       Site Details
              Status Date :                                      2016-04-25
              Status :                                           Open - Eligible for Closure
              Begin Date :                                       2009-10-19
              Global ID :                                        T10000001598
              Region :                                           REGION 2

              Site History :

                      Due to a corporate relocation out of state in 2008 the Western Forge and Flange facility closure was initiated and
                      included a subsurface investigation due to potential concerns relative to previous site processes employed at the
                      site. A series of investigations were conducted, and based on the results, a number of free phase hydraulic oil
                      releases and metals contamination in soil and groundwater were documented. Remedial excavations were
                      conducted in October and November 2013, and three monitoring wells were subsequently installed to monitor and
                      sample groundwater in order to determine if the remedial overexcavation successfully removed associated
                      contamination. An historic rail line, and historic fill and associated contamination, was encountered during the
                      excavations and both were subsequently removed to the limits of the property. Limited residual contamination
                      above identified remedial goals is present and a Site Management Plan has been generated in order to manage
                      subsurface incursions, and the generation of contaminated soil or groundwater, in the future at the site. The site is
                      scheduled for redevelopment in 2016 by the City of Albany.

FRS (cont.)

              Source Description :                               The Emission Inventory System (EIS) maintains an inventory of large
                                                                 stationary sources and voluntarily-reported smaller sources of air point
                                                                 pollution emitters. It contains information about facility sites and their
                                                                 physical location, emission units, emission processes, release points,
                                                                 control approaches, and regulations. Facility inventory data are kept
                                                                 separate from the emissions data and have stable identifiers to improve
                                                                 continuity from year to year and to help identify duplicate or missing
                                                                 facilities.
                                                                 HWTS-DATAMART provides California with information on hazardous
                                                                 waste shipments for generators, transporters, and treatment, storage,
                                                                 and disposal facilities.

              Source Description :

                      The California Environmental Protection Agency (CalEPA) has recently implemented a new data warehouse system
                      (nSite). This data warehouse combines and merges facility and site information from five different systems
                      managed within CalEPA. The five systems are: California Environmental Reporting System (CERS), EnviroStor,
                      GeoTracker, California Integrated Water Quality System (CIWQS), and Toxic Release Inventory (TRI).


              Source Description :

                      RCRAInfo is EPA’s comprehensive information system that supports the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act
                      (RCRA) of 1976 and the Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments (HSWA) of 1984 through the tracking of events
                      and activities related to facilities that generate, transport, and treat, store, or dispose of hazardous waste.
                      RCRAInfo allows RCRA program staff to track the notification, permit, compliance, and corrective action activities
                      required under RCRA. RCRAInfo also supports generation of the National Hazardous Waste Biennial Report. All
                      generators and treatment, storage, and disposal facilities who handle hazardous waste are required to report to
                      the EPA Administrator at least once every two years to support creation of the Biennial Report.

              Source Description :

                      RCRAInfo is EPA’s comprehensive information system that supports the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act
                      (RCRA) of 1976 and the Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments (HSWA) of 1984 through the tracking of events
                      and activities related to facilities that generate, transport, and treat, store, or dispose of hazardous waste.
                      RCRAInfo allows RCRA program staff to track the notification, permit, compliance, and corrective action activities
                      required under RCRA. RCRAInfo also supports generation of the National Hazardous Waste Biennial Report. All
                      generators and treatment, storage, and disposal facilities who handle hazardous waste are required to report to
                      the EPA Administrator at least once every two years to support creation of the Biennial Report.

   HYDROLOGIC UNIT
   Hydrologic Unit Maps
   USGS
   The United States Geological Survey created a hierarchical system of hydrologic units originally called regions, sub-
   regions, accounting units, and cataloging units. Each unit was assigned a unique Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC). As first
   implemented the system had 21 regions, 221 subregions, 378 accounting units, and 2,264 cataloging units. Over time
   the system was changed and expanded. As of 2010 there are six levels in the hierarchy, represented by hydrologic unit
   codes from 2 to 12 digits long, called regions, subregions, basins, subbasins, watersheds, and subwatersheds. The table
   below describes the system's hydrologic unit levels and their characteristics, along with example names and codes.

City Directory Report
Envirosite's City Directory report is a screening tool designed to assist in evaluating a subject property and possible adjacent properties resulting from past
activities. It includes a search and abstract of available city directories and cross reference directories at five year intervals or the closest available intervals.
Public map sources are reviewed to determine possible adjoining properties to the front, back, left and right of the property.

Environmental Assessment Specialists, Inc. (EAS) has completed a Phase I Environmental Site
Assessment (ESA) for the above referenced site in accordance with the 2021 Master Services Agreement
between EAS and FirstCarbon Solutions (Client), and in substantial compliance with the scope and
limitations of the American Society of Testing Materials (ASTM), Standard Practices for ESAs: The Phase
I ESA Process, Designation E l 527-13.

For the purpose of this report, the entire land area associated with the multiple address and/or multiple
APNs are referred to as the Parent Parcel. The focus of this report, Berkeley Solid Waste & Recycling
Transfer Station (SW&RTS) Replacement Project, is referred to as the Property, Subject Property, and/or
Site; this area is comprised of an approximately 7.36-acre (combined from seven parcels). The existing
developed areas associated with the City of Berkeley Solid Waste Transfer Station and associated Property
operations will be redeveloped over the coming years into an updated and improved waste transfer facility.

The multiple parcel Property is composed of seven parcels (APN 60-2382-3-1, 60-2382-3-3, 60- 2382-1-
2, 60-2362-1-10, 60-2362-1-11, 60-2362-1-9 and 60-2362-1-8) is located at 1203 Second Street in
Berkeley, Alameda County, California. The City of Berkeley also operates the commercial collection
program which collects recyclables from commercial establishments throughout the city (including multi-
family with 10 or more units as well as businesses). Together, the programs collect refuse, recyclables and
green/food waste materials. The City-owned facility provides operations yards and buildings for the
following: (1) Ecology Center, which operates the City’s residential curbside collection recycling program
for single and multi-family up to nine (9) units, and (2) the Community Conservation Centers, Inc. (CCC),
operates the City’s “Berkeley Recycling”, which includes public drop-off of recyclables and some
universal waste material centers; operates a CRV; and operates a material recovery facility to sort and
market all recyclables delivered to the facility as part of the City’s and Ecology Center curbside recycling
collection program. Per the Alameda County Assessor’s office, the combined seven Parent Parcel Group
is 7.4897-acres. The seven Parent Parcel Group is occupied by the following operations:
      • Trillium Natural Gas filing station (1101 Second Street)
              o Drive up facility of City owned vehicles and public vehicles for compressed natural gas
                 vehicle filling. Above grade cylinders hold natural gas.
      • Berkeley Transfer Station (1201 Second Street)
              o The Berkeley Transfer Station accepts commercial and residential waste along with
                 Compostable Yard Waste, carpet, mattresses, construction and demolition materials,
                 appliances, waste oil and/or but not limited to metals from the City of Berkeley as well
                 as surrounding cities. Depending on the waste material imported to the transfer
                 station, each vehicle pays a rate after being weighed. Hazardous materials are not
                 accepted along with e-waste, and/or but not limited to treated

                     pressurized wood. Additional Berkeley Transfer Station activities include the
                     following: Diesel fueling operations (two dispenser islands connected to two
                     underground storage tanks, a Truck Wash bay with a collection sump, offices,
                     truck parking, a City of Berkeley self-support wireless tower with an attached
                     diesel generator, a machine shop, outdoor storage a large vehicle garage service
                     area with above grade solvent wash racks, a large refuse building utilized to
                     transfer the waste from the public to a drop area where diesel semi-trucks pick
                     up the waste for off property disposal, movable containers for various collected
                     waste storage, and an engineered stormwater drain with an oil waste separator.
      • Ecology Center, Inc. (1231 Second Street)

              California Container Redemption Value (CRV) buyback center that buys redeemable
              containers and provides for drop-off of recyclables. The following are programs
              operated by CCC: paper recycling, glass recycling, various metal recycling, and plastic
              recycling as well as baling operations. All collected recycling materials are transported
              off Property for recycling into new or similar products.

The Property is accessible via paved access driveways located along Second Street and Gillman Street.
The Property is located in an area comprised primarily of commercial and industrial uses with limited
nearby residential improvements. EAS walked the Property, visually observing all accessible features. At
the time of the site visit, the Property appeared to be in fair condition with several buildings and operations
appearing to show deferred maintenance. For example, the main covered collection building at the
Berkeley Transfer Station has numerous holes in the roof allowing rainwater to leak inside the refuse
collection area. Additionally, the walls of the Berkeley Transfer Station building have been damaged with
heavy equipment use. The main Berkeley Transfer Station covered collection building gutter rainwater
system also has numerous holes. The asphalt around the Subject Property yards is uneven with rainwater
ponding and flow to the City of Berkeley sidewalk and storm drain in adjacent streets.

Proposed improvements include the phased removal of numerous buildings at the Property, grading, and
removal of historical foundations to facilitate the construction of a new Solid Waste & Recycling Transfer
Station. According to the City of Berkeley Solid Waste & Recycling Transfer Station representative, Mr.
Greg Apa, City of Berkeley Solid Waste and Recycling Manager, Zero Waste Division, the Berkeley
Transfer Station started operation in 1983.

Historically, the Property has been continuously developed and utilized in a commercial and or industrial
manner (furniture manufacturing, industrial and medical gas manufacturing and sales, former in-ground
oil storage tanks, former oil and gas operations, former and current machine shops, current diesel dispenser
operations, truck wash rack operations, and a waste soling facility from 1983 through 2021 within an
industrial area of the City of Berkeley from 1901 through 2021 (120 years).

FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

We have performed a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment in general conformance with the scope and
limitations of ASTM Practice El527-13 of the approximately 7.36-acre proposed Solid Waste & Recycling
Transfer Station (SW&RTS) Replacement Project area, located in a seven-parcel project addressed as 1201
Second Street, Berkeley, Alameda County, California, the Property. Any exceptions to, or deletions from,
this practice are described in Section 10.0 of this report. This assessment has revealed evidence of several
recognized environmental conditions in connection with the Property including the following:

Historical Pre-1980 Industrial: Historically prior to the current City of Berkeley development previous
industrial tenant operations from 1901 through 1980 included: machine shops, in-ground oil tanks,
industrial and medical grade gases, oil and gas petroleum operations, and auto outdoor storage operations.
Historical industrial operations typically involve the use of hazardous materials, including solvents and
petroleum products and/or but not limited to various metals. In addition, no documentation was available
indicating whether soil samples were collected and analyzed for the presence of impacted soil. Based on
the length of time that the Property had been industrially utilized prior to 1980, and the absence of data
confirming whether a release had occurred, it is possible that petroleum and or metals may have impacted
the subsurface of the Property. Therefore, the collective historical industrial utilization of the Property from
1901 through 1980 is collectively considered a Recognized Environmental Condition (REC).

Historical Calcium Carbide Ponds to Manufacture Acetylene Gas: The former industrial operation in
the northern portion of the Property operated from the 1920s through the 1970s (Air Reduction Sales
Company per the Sanborn Maps). Apparently, the outdoor large ponds were used to make acetylene by
reacting calcium carbide with water. Calcium carbide can be considered a dangerous and corrosive
chemical. Calcium carbide has cancer causing properties and contains traces of arsenic and phosphorous
hydride. The historical operation of Calcium carbide ponds on the northern portion of the property from
the 1920s through the 1970s may have left residual chemicals and/or metals in the subsurface and is
therefore considered a REC.

Underground Storage Tank (UST) Diesel System: The Subject Property is currently occupied by two
10,000-gallon USTs. The USTs are reportedly single walled and equipped with a leak detection system.
The product piping runs underground from the USTs across a heavily utilized driveway to two separate
pump islands. A visual inspection of each diesel pump dispenser showed heavy petroleum staining at the
base of each unit. As of the date of this report, EAS is awaiting documents form the City of Berkeley Toxic
program regarding inspections and violations, as well as information pertinent to the status and operation
of the current storage tank system. Should receipt of a response from this agency change the conclusions
of this report, the Client will be notified in writing by EAS. Per EDR several violations for monitoring and
UST record keeping were noted. Consequently, based on the lack of continuous documentation indicating
that the UST system has operated in a manner which would prevent or limit the potential for releases, and
the possibility that releases may occur from tanks or tank systems that are otherwise testing as tight, EAS
is unable to rule out the potential that a release from the USTs has affected the subsurface of the Subject
Property. On this basis, the storage of petroleum products in the vicinity of the two pump dispenser islands,
the heavily utilized driveway area between the dispenser island and the USTs, including the two USTs at
the Subject Property are considered a REC as the subsurface may be impacted with petroleum
hydrocarbons.




  Environmental Assessment Specialists, Inc.                                           Office (818) 898-4866
                                                                          Berkeley SW&RTS Replacement Project
                                                                            March 30, 2021 updated July 2, 2021
                                                                                                         Page 5


Truck Wash: A large truck vehicle washing area was observed on the property. A floor drain leading
to an apparent oil/water separator was observed in the concrete floor in the washing area. According
to historical sources, steam cleaning of fleet vehicles and heavy equipment has been performed in this
area since 1983. Due to the subsurface nature of oil/water separators, the potential exists that they may
act as a conduit to the subsurface of the Subject Property for any contaminants released during vehicle
washing and steam cleaning activities such as oil, grease, fuel, or cleaning solvents. Additionally, the
structural integrity of clarifiers and their associated piping to the sewer system can become
compromised over time, especially when located in areas prone to high vehicle traffic. Therefore, the
potential exists that a release from this feature may have resulted in an impact to the subsurface of the
Subject Property. On this basis, the truck wash at the Property is considered a REC as the subsurface
may be impacted with petroleum hydrocarbons, metals, vehicle fluids, etc.

Solid Waste Transfer Facility/ Stormwater Treatment System: The Property's primary use as a solid
waste and recycling transfer station is to accept City collected and third-party delivered refuse, recyclables
and food/green waste materials where these materials are temporarily staged (all materials per permit
removed within 24 hours) and then either sent off Property to a landfill, or recycled and/or composted.
Temporary waste staging areas are in designated areas ofthe Property, in covered and uncovered
locations. Both odors and stormwater runoff from the temporary waste storage is attempted to be collected
through a series of in-ground stormwater collection systems. The stormwater is collected and filtered and
held as needed prior to being transmitted to the city stormwater collection system off the Property.
Stormwater that is not collected runs to adjacent City of Berkley streets and storm drains. As of the date of
this report, EAS is awaiting documents form the City of Berkeley Toxic program regarding inspections
and violations, as well as information pertinent to the status and operation of the current stormwater
treatment system with at least three (3) vaults and 12 storm drain manholes. Should receipt of a response
from this agency change the conclusions of this report, the Client will be notified in writing by EAS. Based
on the above information, the potential exists that a release from this waste stormwater feature may have
resulted in an impact to the subsurface of the Subject Property if seals are not functional or if piping has
become separate with time. The Property has a clear policy of not accepting hazardous waste, however
there is a dedicated area for any inadvertent hazardous waste that has been found within the imported waste.
While most inadvertent hazardous waste may be identified and separated, it can be assumed that not all
hazardous waste has been identified and sorted out (see Collected Hazardous Wastes section below). While
concrete and asphalt surfaces can block particulate matter from leaching to the subsurface, many containers
(if damaged during the loading transfer process) could potentially leak hazardous materials such as
hydrocarbon solvents. Hydrocarbon based solvents have chemical characteristic which allows them to
easily seep through intact or cracked concrete or asphalt surfaces. On this basis, the Solid Waste Transfer-
Stormwater Treatment System facility which has been operational from 1983 through 2021 at the Property
is considered a REC as the subsurface may be impacted with petroleum hydrocarbons and or metals.

Vapor Intrusion: Based on a screening process as outlined by ASTM E 1527, the Property may be located
on, above, or in close proximity to soil or groundwater that has or is indicative of a condition representing
the possibility for Vapor Intrusion based on the presence or likely presence of chemicals of concern (COC)
as listed in the Appendix to ASTM E 1527. A plume associated with the COCs as being identified in
sufficient proximity to the Project is located approximately 100-feet east and upgradient from the Property
as to warrant further assessment. Many areas in the City of Berkeley are known or suspected to have
groundwater contamination. These areas are known as Environmental Management Areas (EMA). As the
Property is located within a City of Berkeley Environmental Management Area, the Toxics Management
Division must be contacted prior to redevelopment activities. Additionally, the upgradient facility to the
east of the Property at 707 Gilman Street (Terminal Manufacturing, LLC) has a solvent impacted
groundwater plume. Elevated concentrations of tetrachloroethene (PCE) and lower concentrations of PCE
biodegradation compounds [trichloroethene (TCE) and cis-1,2-dichloroethene (DCE)], have historically
been observed in groundwater beneath the western portion of the Terminal Manufacturing, LLC facility.
The plume has not been defined, however significant PCE and TCE concentrations are present. The
adjacent and upgradient solvent plume represents both a potential VIC and REC for the Property.

  Environmental Assessment Specialists, Inc.                                         Office (818) 898-4866
                                                                    Berkeley SW&RTS Replacement Project
                                                                      March 30, 2021 updated July 2, 2021
                                                                                                   Page 6


Vehicle Repair and Service Bays: Long-term heavy equipment repair with solvent utilization at
the City of Berkeley heavy truck repair facility from 1983 through 2021. Heavy truck repair
facilities typically store and utilize solvents and petroleum products on-site including hazardous
materials/waste, oil, waste oil, antifreeze, battery acid, grease, antifreeze, and solvent parts
washers (typically containing perchloroethylene). While concrete and asphalt surfaces can block
small particulate matter from leaching to the subsurface, solvents such as (but not limited to)
perchloroethylene, if mishandled, or spilled during working operations could potentially seep
through concrete. Hydrocarbon based solvents have chemical characteristics which allow them
to easily seep through intact or cracked concrete or asphalt surfaces. No current inappropriate
material handling was noted by EAS within the observed four service bays near the large transfer
building. In addition, there are no current in-building sumps or in-ground lifts. Based on the
historic use of the service bays for heavy repair operations (approximately 38 years) and their
continued use until redevelopment, the heavy truck repair operations represent a significant
environmental concern and are a REC for the Property.

Collected Hazardous Wastes
The Property has a clear policy of not accepting hazardous waste, however there is a dedicated
area for any inadvertent hazardous waste that has been found within the imported waste. While
most inadvertent hazardous waste may be identified and separated, it can be assumed that not all
hazardous waste has been identified and sorted out. If not located, the contents of any containers
with hazardous materials would likely be broken during the front wheel loader with bucket
pushing to the tipping station or by other sorting actions so that hazardous materials could be
spilled and spread in various portions of the Property. The Property has been continuously
operated as a transfer station and material recovery (recycling) facility from the early 1980s
through 2021. Based on the historic use of the Property as a waste transfer station and its
continued use until redevelopment, the inadvertent hazardous waste processing and storage is a
significant environmental concern to this assessment as the subsurface could be impacted. The
inadvertent hazardous waste processing and storage is a REC for the Property.

Based on the above information, on-site soils and/or groundwater may contain hazardous materials.
As the Property is to undergo extensive demolition, grading, and/or soil removal during the proposed
redevelopment activities, EAS recommends that subsurface sampling and testing be performed at
the Property prior to any ground disturbance/redevelopment activities including but not limited to:

      • Historical Pre-1980 Industrial (Entire 7 property Parcel)
      • Historical Calcium Carbide Ponds to Manufacture Acetylene Gas (General northern vicinity
        of the Property)
      • UST Diesel System (known designated UST area)
      • Truck Wash (designated area)
      • Solid Waste Disposal Transfer Facility/ Stormwater Treatment System (General northern
        property of the Property)
      • Vapor Intrusion (Entire 7 Parcel Property)
      • Vehicle Repair and Service Bays (General northern portion of the Property)
      • Collected Hazardous Wastes 38-years (Entire 7 Property Parcel)

Once the analysis has been completed, the results would help show whether impacted subsurface
conditions above action levels are present.


  Environmental Assessment Specialists, Inc.                                   Office (818) 898-4866
                                                                 Berkeley SW&RTS Replacement Project
                                                                   March 30, 2021 updated July 2, 2021
                                                                                                Page 7


Of note, the following Business Environmental Risks (BERs) were identified that warrant mention:

      • Based on information obtained from the historical records review, the existing
        improvements were constructed at a time when asbestos-containing materials (ACMs)
        and lead-based paints (LBPs) were still common in building materials. Based on this
        information, there is a potential that ACMs and/or LBPs are present within the on-site
        structures. As the on-site buildings are to be renovated and/or demolished during
        redevelopment activities, EAS recommends that a comprehensive asbestos and lead
        paint survey be conducted prior to any renovation or demolition activities; these
        materials should be characterized for asbestos and lead by a reliable method. All
        activities involving ACMs and LBPs should be conducted in accordance with
        governmental regulations.

In addition, the following items warrant mention:

      • Although microbial growth may occur in a very short time span, an effort was made to
        identify conspicuous microbial growth in the common areas surveyed. In addition, an
        effort was made to observe water damaged building materials, which could indicate
        water intrusion into the structure. No significant areas of microbial growth or water
        intrusion was observed during the site visit. If any areas of microbial growth are
        discovered during redevelopment activities, these materials should be characterized
        by a reliable method. All activities involving microbial growth should be conducted
        in accordance with governmental regulations.
      • Standard dust mitigation measures should be implemented during all redevelopment and
        soil handling activities. During any grading or excavation activities of the Property,
        redevelopment personnel must be made aware to look for unusual conditions suggesting
        buried debris or other potential adverse environmental conditions that may be discovered
        on the Property. In addition, if any abnormal soils are discovered during redevelopment,
        such as stained soils, hydrocarbon odors, or any other unusual odors, construction
        activities should immediately cease and EAS contacted for further assessment and
        monitoring.
      • The Property is located within an historically industrial and commercial area. Many areas
        in the City of Berkeley are known or suspected to have groundwater contamination.
        These areas are known as Environmental Management Areas (EMA). Improper disposal
        of contaminated water or soils can be a violation of the Federal Clean Water Act and
        State Porter Cologne Act, as well as California hazardous Waste Laws. As the Property
        is located within a City of Berkeley Environmental Management Area, the Toxics
        Management Division must be contacted prior to redevelopment activities.

1.0       INTRODUCTION

The purpose of this Phase I ESA was to identify recognized environmental conditions associated with
the Property. To achieve this objective, the Phase I ESA included visual observations of the Property
and observations of the surrounding properties, a visual survey for suspect asbestos­ containing
materials/debris piles/lead-based paint, limited historical land use review, review of regulatory
database listings, and reviews of readily available geologic and hydrogeologic data. This report
represents a summary of these findings. Property maps, site plans, area maps, site photographs,
historical aerial photos and topographic maps, wetlands map, flood hazard map, fire insurance map
report, city directory abstract, regulatory database repo rt, questionnaires, and supporting
documentation are included as attachments to this report.

EAS visited the Property to identify potential sources or indications of chemical contamination such
as underground storage tanks (USTs), aboveground storage tanks (ASTs), polychlorinated biphenyls
(PCBs), chemicals and hazardous waste materials, areas with surficial staining or distressed
vegetation, and visual evidence of asbestos containing materials (ACMs) and/or lead­ based paint.
Lands immediately adjoining to the Property were visually inspected for possible sources of
contamination or environmental impairment, which could migrate to the Site via surface water runoff,
groundwater transport, and other pathways. EAS conducted a regulatory records review, reviewed
historical aerial photographs, historical maps, building permits (upon availability), and contacted and
interviewed property representatives and regulatory agencies, as necessary.

2.0       SITE LOCATION and DESCRIPTION

For the purpose of this report, the entire land area associated with the multiple address and/or multiple
APNs are referred to as the Parent Parcel. The focus of this report (City of Berkeley SW&RTS Replacement
Project) is referred to as the Property, Subject Property, and/or Site; this area is comprised of an
approximately 7.36-acre (combined from seven parcels). The existing developed areas associated with the
Berkley Transfer Station and associated Property operations will be redeveloped over the coming years into
an updated and improve waste transfer facility.

The multiple parcel Property is composed of seven parcels (APN 60-2382-3-1, 60-2382-3-3, 60- 2382-1-

program which collects recyclables from commercial establishments throughout the city (including multi-
family with 10 or more unites as well as businesses). Together, the programs collect refuse, recyclables and
green/food waste materials. The City-owned facility provides operations yards and buildings for the

waste material centers; operates a CRV; and operates a material recovery facility to sort and market all

3.0          PHYSICAL SETTING

Based on the United States Geological Survey (USGS) Richmond, CA 7.5-Minute Quadrangle
(1:24,000), the Property has an average elevation of approximately 13-feet above mean sea level with
slight gradients descending toward the west. Storm water runoff is expected to flow off the Property
to the west.

The Subject Property is located within the northern end of the East Bay Plain, on the eastern flank
of the San Francisco Bay structural trough. The Subject Property is situated approximately one­
half mile east of the eastern shoreline of the San Francisco Bay at an elevation of approximately
13 feet above mean sea level (msl) on a relatively flat to slight westerly sloping topography. The
structural depression that underlies the San Francisco Bay has accumulated up to 1100 feet of
poorly consolidated sediment (Alameda County, 1988). The trough is filled with approximately
950 feet of alluvial fan deposits, characterized by lenticular beds of poorly sorted gravel, sand,
silt, and clay that exhibit wide variations in bed thickness and grain size over short distances.

Information regarding first depth to groundwater and flow direction were researched at the California
Water Resources Control Board's website at https://geot racker.waterboards.ca.gov. According to the
San Francisco Bay region's Basin Plan, groundwater at the site falls within the East Bay Plain
(RWQCB, 1995). Within this basin, the site lies approximately at the dividing line between two
groundwater sub-areas: the Central sub-area, and the Berkeley sub-area. In 1999, the Water Board
completed the "East Bay Plain Groundwater Basin Beneficial Use Evaluation Report" (RWQCB,
1999). After examining the current uses and potential likely future uses of groundwater in this basin,
the Water Board recommended that shallow and deep groundwater in the area of the site (i.e., a portion
of the Central sub-area and the Berkeley sub-area) be designated as Zone B Groundwater Management
Zone. Zone B groundwater is described as "Groundwater unlikely to be used as a drinking water
resource". Groundwater in this category is described as likely to have been used historically as a
domestic water supply (e.g., private wells), but unlikely to be used as public water supply. Regionally,
the ground water flow direction is to the west in the direction of the San Francisco Bay.

Based on previous subsurface investigations performed at the adjoining facility to the east, ground
water has been encountered at depths at around 8 feet below grade surface. Based on a review of
subsurface investigations in the vicinity of the Property, the groundwater flow direction at the subject
site is westerly to southwesterly towards the San Francisco Bay. Seasonal variations, hillside runoff,
aquifer pumping, tidal fluctuations or other factors may influence ground water levels.

4.0          SITE RECONNAISSANCE and OBSERVATION

On March 11, 2021, EAS personnel conducted a site reconnaissance of the Property. The site
reconnaissance is documented in the site photographs (Appendices). The EAS representative was granted
access to the Property by the City of Berkeley Solid Waste Transfer Station representative Mr. Greg Apa,
City of Berkeley Solid Waste and Recycling Manager, Zero Waste Division, but was unaccompanied at the
Property during the site visit. In addition, a walk along the perimeter of the Property and a drive around
roads in the immediate area were conducted. At the time of the site visit, the weather was clear.

The purpose of the site reconnaissance was to visually and physically observe the site, site structures, and
adjoining properties for conditions indicating an existing release, past release, or threatened release of any
hazardous substances or petroleum products into structures of the site, or into soil and/or groundwater
beneath the site. This would include any evidence of contamination, distressed vegetation, petroleum-
hydrocarbon staining, waste drums, illegal dumping, or improper waste storage/handling.

Underground Storage Tanks/Aboveground Storage Tanks (USTs/ASTs) Current USTs and ASTs

Diesel USTs:
The Subject Property is currently occupied by two 10,000-gallon USTs. The USTs are reportedly single
walled and equipped with a leak detection system. The product piping runs underground from the USTs
across a heavily utilized driveway to two separate pump islands. A visual inspection of each diesel pump
dispenser showed heavy petroleum staining at the base of each unit. As of the date of this report, EAS is
awaiting documents from the City of Berkeley Toxic program regarding inspections and violations, as well
as information pertinent to the status and operation of the current storage tank system. Should receipt of a
response from this agency change the conclusions of this report, the Client will be notified in writing by
EAS. Per EDR several violations for monitoring and UST recordkeeping were noted. Consequently, based
on the lack of continuous documentation indicating that the UST system has operated in a manner which
would prevent or limit the potential for releases, and the possibility that releases may occur from tanks or
tank systems that are otherwise testing as tight, EAS is unable to rule out the potential that a release from
the USTs has affected the subsurface of the Subject Property. On this basis, the storage of petroleum
products in the vicinity of the two pump dispenser islands, the heavily utilized driveway area between the
dispenser island and the USTs, including the two USTs at the Subject Property are considered a REC as the
subsurface may be impacted with petroleum hydrocarbons.

Additionally, per local regulations all single wall USTs must be removed by December 21, 2025.

Waste Oil AST:
The Subject Property has one approximately 500-gallon waste oil AST that is covered and has secondary
containment. The waste oil is collected from the public and sent off Property for recycling. Minor staining
was observed at the concrete base of the AST; however, it was not considered significant. At this time, the
waste oil AST is not considered an immediate concern.

Diesel AST for Tower Generator:
The Subject Property has one approximately 90-gallon diesel AST that is connected to the communication
backup emergency generator. Significant stating was not observed in the vicinity of this diesel AST. At this
time, this AST is not considered an immediate concern.

Truck Wash
A large truck vehicle washing area was observed on the Property. A floor drain leading to an apparent
oil/water separator was observed in the concrete floor in the washing area. According to historical
sources, steam cleaning of fleet vehicles and heavy equipment has been performed in this area since
1983. Due to the subsurface nature of oil/water separators, the potential exists that they may act as a
conduit to the subsurface of the Subject Property for any contaminants released during vehicle washing
and steam cleaning activities such as oil, grease, fuel, or cleaning solvents. Additionally, the structural
integrity of clarifiers and their associated piping to the sewer system can become compromised over
time, especially when located in areas prone to high vehicle traffic. Therefore, the potential exists that
a release from this feature may have resulted in an impact to the subsurface of the Subject Property.
On this basis, the truck wash at the Subject Property is considered a REC as the subsurface may be
impacted with petroleum hydrocarbons.

Solid Waste Transfer Facility/ Stormwater Treatment System: The Property's main use is to accept
refuse, recyclables and food/green waste materials so that it can be temporarily stockpiled (all materials per
permit removed within 24 hours) and sent off Property to a landfill, or recycled and/or composted.
Temporary waste piles are located in designated areas of the Property in covered uncovered areas. Both
odors and stormwater runoff from the temporary waste storage is attempted to be collected through a series
of in-ground stormwater collection systems. The stormwater is collected and filtered and held as needed
prior to being transmitted to the city stormwater collection system off the Property. Stormwater that is not
collected runs to adjacent City of Berkley streets and storm drains. As of the date of this report, EAS is
awaiting documents form the City of Berkeley Toxic program regarding inspections and violations, as well
as information pertinent to the status and operation of the current stormwater treatment system with at least
three (3) vaults and 12 storm drain manholes. Should receipt of a response from this agency change the
conclusions of this report, the Client will be notified in writing by EAS. Based on the above information,
the potential exists that a release from this waste stormwater feature may have resulted in an impact to the
subsurface of the Subject Property if seals are not functional or if piping has become separate with time. It
should be noted that hazardous materials are not accepted at the property. However a hazardous material
collection area is operational which is used as a designated covered storage area encountered hazardous
waste materials. While the transfer station does not complete sorting, intentional and/or unintentional
hazardous waste containers (if visually encountered) are apparently collected, sorted and placed at the
property in a designated Hazardous Waste collection area. While concrete and asphalt surfaces can block
particulate matter from leaching to the subsurface many containers if damaged during the loading transfer
process could potentially leak hazardous materials such as hydrocarbon solvents. Hydrocarbon based
solvents have chemical characteristic which allows them to easily seep through intact or cracked concrete
or asphalt surfaces. On this basis, the Solid Waste Transfer facility which has been operational from 1983
through 2021/ Stormwater Treatment System at the Property is considered a REC as the subsurface may be
impacted with petroleum hydrocarbons and or metals.

Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs)

not observed by EAS in the vicinity of the transformers.

Waste Management and Chemical

Vehicle Repair and Service Bays
Long-term heavy equipment repair with solvent utilization at the City of Berkeley heavy truck
repair facility from 1983 through 2021. Heavy truck repair facilities typically store and utilize
solvents and petroleum products on-site including hazardous materials/waste, oil, waste oil,
antifreeze, battery acid, grease, antifreeze, and solvent parts washers (typically containing
perchloroethylene). While concrete and asphalt surfaces can block small particulate matter from
leaching to the subsurface, solvents such as but not limited to perchloroethylene if mishandled or
spilled during working operations could potentially seep through concrete. Hydrocarbon based
solvents have chemical characteristic which allows them to easily seep through intact or cracked
concrete or asphalt surfaces. No current inappropriate material handling was noted by EAS within
the observed four service bays near the large transfer building. In addition, there are no current
in-building sumps or in-ground lifts. Based on the historic use of the service bays for heavy repair
operations (approximately 38 years) and their continued use until redevelopment, the heavy truck
repair operations represent a significant environmental concern/ REC for the Property.

Collected Hazardous Wastes
The Property has a clear policy of not accepting hazardous waste, however there is a dedicated
area for any inadvertent hazardous waste that has been found within the imported waste. While
most inadvertent hazardous waste is likely identified and separated, it can be assumed that not all
of such waste materials has been identified and sorted out. If not located, the contents of any
containers with hazardous materials would likely be broken during operations by the front wheel
loader with bucket pushing waste debris from the tipping floor to the load out chute and into
transfer trailers or by other sorting actions, creating the potential for hazardous materials to be
spilled and spread in various portions of the Property. The Property has been continuously
operated as a transfer station and material recovery (recycling) facility from the early 1980s
through 2021. Based on the historic and continued use of the Property as a waste transfer station,
the inadvertent hazardous waste processing and storage is a significant environmental concern to
this assessment as the subsurface could be impacted. The inadvertent hazardous waste processing
and storage is a REC for the Property.

Underground Oil or Gas Pipelines

Two Kinder Morgan hydrocarbon pipelines are located in the adjacent Union Pacific Railroad's railway
area to the east. One of the two pipelines is located within approximately 15 feet of the entire eastern
boundary of the Property. While hydrocarbon pipelines can be a concern, the responsibility of any releases
would lie with the owner Kinder Morgan.

Asbestos-Containing Material ACM and Lead-Based Paint (LBP)

Based on information obtained from the historical records review, the existing improvements were
constructed at a time when asbestos-containing materials (ACMs) and lead-based paints (LBPs) were
still common in building materials. Based on this information, there is a potential that ACMs and/or
LBPs are present within the on-site structures. As the on-site buildings are to be renovated and/or
demolished during redevelopment activities, EAS recommends that a comprehensive asbestos and lead
paint survey be conducted prior to any renovation or demolition activities; these materials should be
characterized for asbestos and lead by a reliable method. All activities involving ACMs and LBPs
should be conducted in accordance with governmental regulations.

debris so that all surface areas could not be assessed. Only limited landscaping is located along Gilman

during the site reconnaissance .

Pits, Ponds, or Lagoons

Radon

Radon gas is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that is invisible and odorless. It forms from the
radioactive decay of small amounts of uranium and thorium naturally present in rocks and soils, so
some radon exists in all rocks and soils. Because radon is a gas, it can easily move through soil and
cracks in building slabs or basement walls and concentrate in a building's indoor air. According to the
government database Federal EPA Radon Zone for Alameda County (http://www.city-data.co
m/radon-zones/California/California.html), six (6) radon tests have taken place in sites located within
the Property's zip code of 94710 and zero (0) tests came back positive for radon levels of 4 picocuries
per liter (pCi/L) or above, which is the state of California's recommended action level. Alameda
County is listed in Radon Zone 2 (Moderate Potential), counties that have a predicted average indoor
radon screening level between 2 and 4 pCi /L. Based on this information, the presence of on-site radon
levels above California's recommended action level is unlikely.

been under regulatory oversight management for past and current operations with violations and former
petroleum LUST releases noted. The former LUST did receive closure in 1997. Based on the EAS
assessment work completed in other sections of this report, in addition to the Property being located within
a designated City of Berkeley Environmental Management Area (EMA) with subsurface impacts assumed
to be present, the collective assortment of regulatory listings is a potential concern for the Property. Please
see Section 1.0 of this assessment for a listing the identified RECs and potential environmental concerns.

commercial-industrial with Public Storage to the north and industrial welding supply to the south, a waste
transfer station across 2nd Street, and a foundry to the south across Gilman Street. Weatherford BMW
has developed the site and is operating it as an automobile repair shop.

City of Berkeley Environmental Management Areas

The Property is located within an historically industrial and commercial area. Berkeley's soils and
groundwater have been adversely impacted by past industrial and commercial activities, as well as by
leaded gasoline, lead paint, and leaking sewers. Toxics Management Division (TMD) staff will review
the project description or plans and determine if special requirements should apply. Requirements are
applicable for significant soils movements or removal, and where excavation may encounter
groundwater. Many areas in the City of Berkeley are known or suspected to have groundwater
contamination. These areas are known as Environmental Management Areas (EMA). Improper
disposal of contaminated water or soils can be a violation of the Federal Clean Water Act and State
Poiter Cologne Act, as well as California Hazardous Waste Laws. As the Property is located within a
City of Berkeley Environmental Management Area, the Toxics Management Division must be
contacted prior to redevelopment activities.

8.0          HISTORICAL USE INFORMATION REVIEW

Vapor Intrusion Condition (VIC)

Based on a screening process as outlined by ASTM E 1527, the Property may be located on, above, or in
close proximity to soil or groundwater that has or is indicative of a condition representing the possibility
for Vapor Intrusion based on the presence or likely presence of chemicals of concern (COC) as listed in the
Appendix to ASTM E 1527. A plume associated with the COCs as being identified in sufficient proximity
to the Project (within 100-feet east) is located upgradient from the Property as to warrant further assessment.

Additionally, The Property is located within an historically industrial and commercial area. Many areas in
the City of Berkeley are known or suspected to have groundwater contamination. These areas are known
as Environmental Management Areas (EMA). As the Property is located within a City of Berkeley
Environmental Management Area, the Toxics Management Division must be contacted prior to
redevelopment activities.

Additionally, the upgradient facility to the east of the Property at 707 Gilman Street (Terminal
Manufacturing, LLC) has a solvent impacted groundwater plume. Elevated concentrations of
tetrachloroethene (PCE) and lower concentrations of PCE biodegradation compounds [trichloroethene
(TCE) and cis-1,2-dichloroethene (DCE)], have historically been observed in groundwater beneath the
western portion of the Terminal Manufacturing, LLC facility. The plume has not been defined,
however significant PCE and TCE concentrations are present. The adjacent and upgradient solvent
plume represents both a potential VIC and REC for the Property.

9.0       FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

We have performed a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment in general conformance with the scope and
limitations of ASTM Practice El 527-13 of the approximately 7.36-acre proposed Berkeley SW&RTS
Replacement Project area, located in a seven-parcel project addressed as 1201 Second Street, Berkeley,
Alameda County, California, the Property. Any exceptions to, or deletions from, this practice are described
in Section 10.0 of this report. This assessment has revealed evidence of several recognized environmental
conditions in connection with the Property including the following:

Historical Pre-1980 Industrial: Historically, prior to the current City of Berkeley development, previous
industrial tenant operations from 1901 through 1980 included: machine shops, in-ground oil tanks,
industrial and medical grade gases, oil and gas petroleum operations, and auto outdoor storage operations.
Historical industrial operations typically involve the use of hazardous materials, including solvents and
petroleum products and/or but not limited to various metals. In addition, no documentation was available
indicating whether soil samples were collected and analyzed for the presence of impacted soil. Based on
the length of time that the Property had been industrially utilized prior to 1980, and the absence of data
confirming whether a release had occurred, it is possible that petroleum and or metals may have impacted
the subsurface of the Property. Therefore, the collective historical industrial utilization of the Property from
1901 through 1980 is collectively considered a Recognized Environmental Condition (REC).

Historical Calcium Carbide Ponds to Manufacture Acetylene Gas: The former industrial operation in
the northern portion of the Property operated from the 1920s through the 1970s (Air Reduction Sales
Company per the Sanborn Maps). Apparently, the outdoor large ponds were used to make acetylene by
reacting calcium carbide with water. Calcium carbide can be considered a dangerous and corrosive
chemical. Calcium carbide has cancer causing properties and contains traces of arsenic and phosphorous
hydride. The historical operation of Calcium Carbide ponds on the northern portion of the property from
the 1920s through the 1970s may have left residual chemicals and/or metals in the subsurface and is
therefore considered a REC.

Underground Storage Tank (UST) Diesel System: The Subject Property is currently occupied by two
10,000-gallon USTs. The USTs are reportedly single walled and equipped with a leak detection system.
The product piping runs underground from the USTs across a heavily utilized driveway to two separate
pump islands. A visual inspection of each diesel pump dispenser showed heavy petroleum staining at the
base of each unit. As of the date of this report, EAS is awaiting documents form the City of Berkeley Toxic
program regarding inspections and violations, as well as information pertinent to the status and operation
of the current storage tank system. Should receipt of a response from this agency change the conclusions
of this report, the Client will be notified in writing by EAS. Per EDR several violations for monitoring and
UST record keeping were noted. Consequently, based on the lack of continuous documentation indicating
that the UST system has operated in a manner which would prevent or limit the potential for releases, and
the possibility that releases may occur from tanks or tank systems that are otherwise testing as tight, EAS
is unable to rule out the potential that a release from the USTs has affected the subsurface of the Subject
Property. On this basis, the storage of petroleum products in the vicinity of the two pump dispenser islands,
the heavily utilized driveway area between the dispenser island and the USTs, including the two USTs at
the Subject Property are considered a REC as the subsurface may be impacted with petroleum
hydrocarbons.




  Environmental Assessment Specialists, Inc.                                           Office (818) 898-4866
                                                                         Berkeley SW&RTS Replacement Project
                                                                            March 30, 2021 updated July 2, 2021
                                                                                                       Page 27


Truck Wash: A large truck vehicle washing area was observed on the Property. A floor drain leading
to an apparent oil/water separator was observed in the concrete floor in the washing area. According
to historical sources, steam cleaning of fleet vehicles and heavy equipment has been performed in this
area since 1983. Due to the subsurface nature of oil/water separators, the potential exists that they
may act as a conduit to the subsurface of the Subject Property for any contaminants released during
vehicle washing and steam cleaning activities such as oil, grease, fuel, or cleaning solvents.
Additionally, the structural integrity of clarifiers and their associated piping to the sewer system can
become compromised over time, especially when located in areas prone to high vehicle traffic.
Therefore, the potential exists that a release from this feature may have resulted in an impact to the
subsurface of the Subject Property. On this basis, the truck wash at the Property is considered a REC
as the subsurface may be impacted with petroleum hydrocarbons, metals, vehicle fluids, etc.

Solid Waste Transfer Facility/ Stormwater Treatment System: The Property's main use is to accept
refuse, recyclables and food/green waste materials so that it can be temporarily stockpiled (all materials
per permit removed within 24 hours) and sent off Property to a landfill, or are recycled and/or composted.
Temporary waste piles are located on the Property in covered and uncovered areas. Both odors and
stormwater runoff from the temporary waste storage is attempted to be collected through a series of in-
ground stormwater collection systems. The stormwater is collected and filtered and held as needed prior to
being transmitted to the city stormwater collection system off the Property. Stormwater that is not collected
runs to adjacent City of Berkley streets and storm drains. As of the date of this report, EAS is awaiting
documents form the City of Berkeley Toxic program regarding inspections and violations, as well as
information pertinent to the status and operation of the current stormwater treatment system with at least
three (3) vaults and 12 storm drain manholes. Should receipt of a response from this agency change the
conclusions of this report, the Client will be notified in writing by EAS. Based on the above information,
the potential exists that a release from this waste stormwater feature may have resulted in an impact to the
subsurface of the Subject Property if seals are not functional or if piping has become separate with time.
The Property has a clear policy of not accepting hazardous waste, however there is a dedicated area for
any inadvertent hazardous waste that has been found within the imported waste. While most inadvertent
hazardous waste may be identified and separated, it can be assumed that not all hazardous waste has been
identified and sorted out (see Collected Hazardous Wastes section below). While concrete and asphalt
surfaces can block particulate matter from leaching to the subsurface, many containers (if damaged during
the loading transfer process) could potentially leak hazardous materials such as hydrocarbon solvents.
Hydrocarbon based solvents have chemical characteristic which allows them to easily seep through intact
or cracked concrete or asphalt surfaces. On this basis, the Solid Waste Transfer facility-Stormwater
Treatment System which has been operational from 1983 through 2021 at the Property is considered a REC
as the subsurface may be impacted with petroleum hydrocarbons and or metals.

Vapor Intrusion: Based on a screening process as outlined by ASTM E 1527, the Property may be
located on, above, or in close proximity to soil or groundwater that has or is indicative of a condition
representing the possibility for Vapor Intrusion based on the presence or likely presence of chemicals
of concern (COC) as listed in the Appendix to ASTM E 1527. A plume associated with the COCs as
being identified in sufficient proximity to the Project is located approximately 100-feet east and
upgradient from the Property as to warrant further assessment. Many areas in the City of Berkeley are
known or suspected to have groundwater contamination. These areas are known as Environmental
Management Areas (EMA). As the Property is located within a City of Berkeley Environmental
Management Area, the Toxics Management Division must be contacted prior to redevelopment
activities. Additionally, the upgradient facility to the east of the Property at 707 Gilman Street
(Terminal Manufacturing, LLC) has a solvent impacted groundwater plume. Elevated concentrations
of tetrachloroethene (PCE) and lower concentrations of PCE biodegradation compounds
[trichloroethene (TCE) and cis-1,2-dichloroethene (DCE)], have historically been observed in
groundwater beneath the western portion of the Terminal Manufacturing, LLC facility. The plume
has not been defined, however significant PCE and TCE concentrations are present. The adjacent and
upgradient solvent plume represents both a potential VIC and REC for the Property.
Environmental Assessment Specialists, Inc.                                          Office (818) 898-4866
                                                                    Berkeley SW&RTS Replacement Project
                                                                       March 30, 2021 updated July 2, 2021
                                                                                                  Page 28


Vehicle Repair and Service Bays: Long-term heavy equipment repair with solvent utilization at
the City of Berkeley heavy truck repair facility from 1983 through 2021. Heavy truck repair
facilities typically store and utilize solvents and petroleum products on-site including hazardous
materials/waste, oil, waste oil, antifreeze, battery acid, grease, antifreeze, and solvent parts
washers (typically containing perchloroethylene). While concrete and asphalt surfaces can block
small particulate matter from leaching to the subsurface, solvents such as but not limited to
perchloroethylene if mishandled or spilled during working operations could potentially seep
through concrete. Hydrocarbon based solvents have chemical characteristic which allows them
to easily seep through intact or cracked concrete or asphalt surfaces. No current inappropriate
material handling was noted by EAS within the observed four service bays near the large transfer
building. In addition, there are no current in-building sumps or in-ground lifts. Based on the
historic use of the service bays for heavy repair operations (approximately 38 years) and their
continued use until redevelopment, the heavy truck repair operations represent a significant
environmental concern and are a REC for the Property.

Collected Hazardous Wastes
The Property has a clear policy of not accepting hazardous waste, however there is a dedicated
area for any inadvertent hazardous waste that has been found within the imported waste. While
most inadvertent hazardous waste may be identified and separated, it can be assumed that not all
hazardous waste has been identified and sorted out. If not located, the contents of any containers
with hazardous materials would likely be broken during the front wheel loader with bucket
pushing from the tipping floor to the load out chute and into transfer trailers or by other sorting
actions so that hazardous materials could be spilled and spread in various portions of the Property.
The Property has been continuously operated as a transfer station and material recovery
(recycling) facility from the early 1980s through 2021. Based on the historic use of the Property
as a waste transfer station and its continued use until redevelopment, the inadvertent hazardous
waste processing and storage is a significant environmental concern to this assessment as the
subsurface could be impacted. The inadvertent hazardous waste processing and storage is a REC
for the Property.

Based on the above information, on-site soils and/or groundwater may contain hazardous materials.
As the Property is to undergo extensive demolition, grading, and/or soil removal during the proposed
redevelopment activities, EAS recommends that subsurface sampling and testing be performed at
the Property prior to any ground disturbance/redevelopment activities including but not limited to:

      • Historical Pre-1980 Industrial (Entire 7 property Parcel)
      • Historical Calcium Carbide Ponds to Manufacture Acetylene Gas (General northern vicinity
        of the Property)
      • UST Diesel System (known designated UST area)
      • Truck Wash (designated area)
      • Solid Waste Disposal Transfer Facility/ Stormwater Treatment System (General northern
        portion of the Property)
      • Vapor Intrusion (Entire 7 Parcel Property)
      • Vehicle Repair and Service Bays (General northern portion property of the Property)
      • Collected Hazardous Wastes 38-years (Entire 7 property Parcel)

Once the analysis has been completed, the results would help show whether impacted subsurface
conditions above action levels are present.

Of note, the following Business Environmental Risks (BERs) were identified that warrant mention:

      • Based on information obtained from the historical records review, the existing
        improvements were constructed at a time when asbestos-containing materials (ACMs)
        and lead-based paints (LBPs) were still common in building materials. Based on this
        information, there is a potential that ACMs and/or LBPs are present within the on-site
        structures. As the on-site buildings are to be renovated and/or demolished during
        redevelopment activities, EAS recommends that a comprehensive asbestos and lead
        paint survey be conducted prior to any renovation or demolition activities; these
        materials should be characterized for asbestos and lead by a reliable method. All
        activities involving ACMs and LBPs should be conducted in accordance with
        governmental regulations.

In addition, the following items warrant mention:

      • Although microbial growth may occur in a very short time span, an effort was made to
        identify conspicuous microbial growth in the common areas surveyed. In addition, an
        effort was made to observe water damaged building materials, which could indicate
        water intrusion into the structure. No significant areas of microbial growth or water
        intrusion was observed during the site visit. If any areas of microbial growth are
        discovered during redevelopment activities, these materials should be characterized
        by a reliable method. All activities involving microbial growth should be conducted
        in accordance with governmental regulations.
      • Standard dust mitigation measures should be implemented during all redevelopment and
        soil handling activities. During any grading or excavation activities of the Property,
        redevelopment personnel must be made aware to look for unusual conditions suggesting
        buried debris or other potential adverse environmental conditions that may be discovered
        on the Property. In addition, if any abnormal soils are discovered during redevelopment,
        such as stained soils, hydrocarbon odors, or any other unusual odors, construction
        activities should immediately cease and EAS contacted for further assessment and
        monitoring.
      • The Property is located within an historically industrial and commercial area. Many areas
        in the City of Berkeley are known or suspected to have groundwater contamination.
        These areas are known as Environmental Management Areas (EMA). Improper disposal
        of contaminated water or soils can be a violation of the Federal Clean Water Act and
        State Porter Cologne Act, as well as California Hazardous Waste Laws. As the Property
        is located within a City of Berkeley Environmental Management Area, the Toxics
        Management Division must be contacted prior to redevelopment activities.

10.0      LIMITATIONS

This Phase I Environmental Site Assessment focused on the proposed City of Berkeley SW&RTS
Replacement Project area and its relationship to any on-site Recognized Environmental
Conditions, if any. It is up to the Client, based on their risk tolerance and applicable law, to
determine the extent of further inquiry. The professional opinions contained in this report are
based solely on the laws, regulations, and technical data known to EAS at the time of report
preparation. The conclusions of this assessment rely on reasonably obtainable information from site
reconnaissance, interviews with on-site personnel and public officials, and public records. No
warranty is made regarding the accuracy of the publicly documented information or the opinions of
officials or personnel consulted for the study. All known information has been disclosed and a
good-faith effort has been made to consult pertinent sources.

It should be noted that all environmental assessments are inherently limited in the sense that
conclusions are drawn, and recommendations developed, from information obtained from limited
research and site evaluation. Subsurface conditions were not investigated as part of this study and may
differ from the conditions implied by visual observations. Additionally, the passage of time may result
in a change in environmental characteristics at this site and on surrounding properties. This report
does not warrant against future operations, activities, or conditions that may occur. This report is not
a regulatory compliance audit. A regulatory compliance audit of the tenant operation would analyze
compliance of the operation with regulatory requirements and accepted industry practices. The scope
of the Phase I ESA focused on the likelihood or potential presence of recognized environmental
conditions at the Subject Property, according to ASTM standards.

This study is not intended to assess or otherwise determine if any soil contamination, waste
emplacement, or groundwater contamination exists on the Subject Property. This investigation
has been based only upon prior site history, previous documentation, and observable conditions.
Existing hazardous materials and contaminants can escape detection using these methods. If the
results of this study suggest that it is possible that hazardous materials contamination exists at the
Subject Property, then further investigation (regulatory file review, subsurface testing) may be
necessary to make a definite assessment. Our conclusions regarding the potential environmental
impact from off-site facilities near the Subject Property are based on readily available information
from the environmental databases and the assumed groundwater flow direction. A detailed file
review of each facility was beyond the scope of work.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The purpose of this work was to obtain information and complete new site investigation efforts
in support of the design of a feasible, in-situ, groundwater treatment program. Stellar
Environmental Solutions (Stellar Environmental) was retained by Terminal Engineering and
Manufacturing (TEM) to develop a plan for the application of injected bioremediation
compounds to reduce volatile organic compounds (VOCs) recognized at 707 Gilman Street
property in Berkeley, California. The work described in this report was generally performed in
accordance with the Water Board-approved workplan, “Workplan and Feasibility Assessment to
Implement PCE Corrective Actions towards VOC Site Closure” (Workplan) dated September 14,
2017. The Water Board provided their approval of the Stellar Environmental Workplan on
September 22, 2018. The Water Board’s approval included a request that the first documentation
report cover the site investigations, well installation, baseline sampling, and final injection
design considerations.

Work completed as documented in this report include, a Membrane Interface Probe (MIP)
investigation including six locations to depths of 40 feet below grade (fbg) and 1 to 50 fbg in the
location of previously-detected elevated concentrations of tetrachloroethene (PCE) in
groundwater. The MIP work guided the placement of three sets of nested wells placed in shallow
and deeper water-bearing zones. Shallow and deep grab-groundwater samples were obtained
from an offsite, downgradient, location. The nested well pairs were permitted and inspected,
developed, surveyed, and sampled. The reporting of this work includes an updated conceptual
site model and final in-situ remediation design. Two MIPs probes were also located west of the
railway line downgradient of the Site to evaluate the extent of VOC attenuation in that direction.

This investigation provided sufficient definition of subsurface conditions to support the design
and implementation of an in-situ media application to reduce VOC impacts to the groundwater.
Contaminant distribution, groundwater flow conditions, and appropriate groundwater attenuation
conditions are favorable for the in-situ application of injectable media. The treatment application
plan (TAP) design is included in this report. Future groundwater monitoring from the nested well
network will be used to evaluate the effect of the selected treatment media application to reduce
PCE and related VOC impacts to groundwater.

REGULATORY CONSIDERATIONS

The Water Board has established Environmental Screening Levels (ESL) for evaluating the
likelihood of environmental impact. ESLs were developed as the lowest screening values for


Stellar Environmental Solutions                                                             Page v
COCs that might be indicative of site source origin and/or pose a significant risk to human health
or the environment, assuming all possible exposure pathways. ESLs are conservative screening-
level criteria published for soil, groundwater, soil-gas, and indoor air—designed to be generally
protective of both drinking water resources and aquatic environments, they incorporate both
environmental and human health risk considerations. ESLs are not cleanup criteria (i.e., health-
based numerical values or disposal-based values). Rather, they are used as a preliminary guide in
determining whether remediation and/or investigation may be warranted. Exceedance of ESLs
suggests that additional investigation and/or remediation is warranted. However, because some
environmental and human health concerns considered in determining ESLs may not be
applicable where exposure routes are not complete, soil that exceeds ESLs does not necessarily
pose a significant risk to human health or the environment.

The February 2016 updated ESLs were used to compare the site data against, as is shown in the
data tables. While some areas groundwater is more sensitive to impact due to it being used, the
current ESLs do not distinguish between sites where groundwater is a potential drinking water
resource or is not as likely to be a drinking a water resource. Based on the subject property
location and the East Bay Plains Report designation of local groundwater use being unlikely to
be used, the risk to groundwater resources would not be as great as in the case of where there are
more sensitive groundwater use concerns. However, the February 2016 ESL updates use the
default ESL value of the drinking water standard for a given analyte. Thus for this site:
 Commercial/industrial land use based upon the current zoning by the City of Berkeley.

 The groundwater ESL for the principal CVOC COC, PCE is 5 micrograms per liter (µg/L),
    the drinking water standard for PCE, although the Water Board Low Threat Closure Policy
    (LTCP) iniative for CVOC sites allows for site closures to occur on a given property with
    higher than the ESL value when the LTCP criteria is satisfied.
 The receiving body for groundwater discharge is an estuary (San Francisco Bay).

The State of California has also promulgated drinking water standards (maximum contaminant
levels [MCLs]) for some of the site contaminants. Drinking water standards may also be utilized
by regulatory agencies to evaluate the potential risk associated with groundwater contamination.
For the site contaminants, MCLs are generally the same as the ESLs. When ESLs or drinking
water standards are exceeded at a site, additional investigative and/or corrective actions are
normally recommended by the regulator to define the impacts. These actions are driven by the
potential risk associated with the contaminant(s) and investigation and corrective actions are
used to demonstrate no significant potential risk to sensitive receptors in the case of sites where
drinking water is not threatened.

In December 2004, the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) on behalf
of the California Environmental Protection Agency (Cal EPA) established their own risk

Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                      Page vi
comparable to the Water Boards ESLs, which are called California Human Health Screening
Levels (CHHSLs). The Water Board also established their equivalents of the CHHSL, the ESLs
that were most recently updated in December 2013. The concentrations from this survey are
compared to the Water Board February 2016 ESLs guidance as that has superseded the DTSC
CHHSLs, which are no longer being updated.

The California Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Cal OSHA) has also established
permissible exposure limits (PELs) that reflect the maximum permitted 8-hour average
concentration limit of an airborne contaminant associated with a given industry. The PELs are to
be applied to occupational exposure (such as exposure to dry cleaner chemicals for workers at
dry cleaners or petroleum exposure for workers at a petroleum service station) and are not
applicable in this case. The Cal OSHA standards, while more conservative, are similar to the
federal OSHA standards. Both the Cal OSHA standards and federal standards are law versus
guidance and are significantly less conservative than the Cal EPA Water Board ESLs or DTSC
used CHHSL values.

assigned Water Board Fuel Leak Case No. 01-3630 and CA GeoTracker Global ID
No. T10000006388. Mr. Ralph Lambert, PG, CHG, is the designated Water Board case officer

others, CVOC impacts exceeding ESL and drinking water standards were identified. The Water
Board issued a “Lead Agency Determination for the Property” letter on June 3, 2016 and created

the submission of this report by June 10, 2018.
