1.0    BACKGROUND

BACKGROUND

The property is currently occupied by TEM, located at 707 Gilman Street in Berkeley, California
as shown on Figure 1. TEM designs and fabricates vacuum and pressure vessels, food processing
equipment, and also performs the repair and maintenance of tank trucks. The business was
purchased by TEM in 1988 from a former trucking company that operated four USTs and several
wastewater sumps. The tanks and sumps were all located within the undeveloped strip on the
western side of the TEM property, between the current building and the railroad right-of-way.
The USTs, waste water sumps, and associated piping were closed in 1999. Tank and sump
locations are indicated on the Site Plan, Figure 2. The history of soil and groundwater samples
analyzed for CVOCs are included in Appendix E.

The UST investigations have been completed and the Water Board issued a Site Closure Letter
dated September 12, 2016. The Water Board found the site met all criteria of the Water Board’s
“Low-Threat Underground Storage Tank Case Closure Policy.” The Water Board’s Closure
Letter noted that PCE had been detected in soil vapor and groundwater and subsequently a Site
Cleanup Program (SCP) case, Number 01S0773, was opened to address this condition. Detailed
information regarding the UST site investigation and case closure determination may be found
on the State’s GeoTracker database, case number 01-3630.

Previous historic review and subsurface investigations of on or offsite source or sources of the
PCE impacts recognized at the western margin of the TEM property were unsuccessful. Sanitary
sewer and stormdrain lines were suspect as potential offsite to onsite pathways for impacts
identified at the site. Upgradient sampling locations were used to identify possible onsite
migration from offsite sources, but no significant contributing sources were identified. Onsite
source areas were initially evaluated by the collection of shallow soil samples and grab-
groundwater samples. These efforts were also unsuccessful in discovering definitive locations for
sources originating offsite or as a result of surface infiltration and migration, underground tank
or sump leaks as the source and cause of the impacts recognized in the subsurface; principally in
groundwater.

There has been no identified historic use of PCE at the property, based on interviews with
persons familiar with the recent history of the property and review of City of Berkeley hazardous
materials records. While the use of degreasing agents such as trichloroethylene (TCE) are more
commonly associated with industrial uses, no substantive concentrations of TCE has been found

Stellar Environmental Solutions                                                            Page 1
at the site although it appears occasionally and is suspected as a degradation product of PCE.
PCE is commonly recognized as a dry-cleaning solvent, though it has been found in some
instances to have been used in commercial degreasing operations. Persons familiar with TEM
operations are confident that PCE was never used at the property. Hazardous materials tank truck
repairs have been and are currently being performed at the site. Facility personnel report that
tank contents were sometimes transferred for temporary storage to underground tanks. Records
of tank truck contents or temporary storage are not available. This type of operation was
considered as a potential way for PCE to be introduced into the subsurface. However, as
previously noted, PCE has not been recognized at locations in soil at concentrations confirming
sources originated from recognized sump or underground tank areas.

In an effort to progress the site to closure, Stellar Environmental approached the PCE-impact
scenario as an apparent non-point-sourced release with characteristics suggesting zones of
elevated PCE concentrations in general association with historic locations of sumps and
underground tanks. The use and operation of the sumps is uncertain. The underground tanks
were reported to have stored fuels and used oil and that one or more of the tanks had been
historically used to for the temporary storage of tank-truck contents during typical service
operations. The distribution of CVOCs in groundwater shows some coincidence with former
underground tank and sump locations, however soil sampling from these locations did not
identify these areas as definitive sources.

CVOC contamination was not found in soil immediately above the highest groundwater VOC
contamination in the northern and southern areas of the western facility support areas (where the
former USTs were located). The far lower concentration in soil compared to groundwater could
reflect either the location of the shallow contamination that originated at the surface has not been
discovered or the leaks/spills are older where the shallow CVOC had time to volatilize and the
CVOCs found at depth have had sufficient time to migrate to the deeper groundwater. The origin
of the CVOCs in groundwater could have been through former USTs, sumps or surface leaks or
other sources.

PCE is present at elevated concentrations in groundwater near and beneath the TEM property.
The distribution of PCE is addressed in this report as two groundwater zones. Membrane
Interface Probe (MIP) logging was employed during this investigation to provide rapid data
regarding the subsurface conditions. The PCE concentration gradient between these zones is
significant, with the deeper zone exhibiting significantly higher concentrations, suggesting Dense
Non Aqueous Phase Liquid (DNAPL) may have been present in the past and migrated to depth
before defusing. Groundwater distributions in the deeper groundwater zone appear to have a
similar footprint to previously described distributions of petroleum hydrocarbon concentrations
as reported previously by Stellar Environmental and others.



Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                        Page 2
No significant pathways of exposure have been identified, either to onsite workers or to offsite
human or environmental receptors. During this investigation onsite PCE concentrations in the
shallow and deeper groundwater-bearing zones showed a maximum of 170 micrograms per liter
(µg/L) and 4,300 µg/L, respectively. Downgradient and offsite grab-groundwater samples were
reported with PCE concentrations in the shallow and deeper zone of not detected above the
laboratory limit of detection of 0.5 µg/L and 150 µg/L, respectively.

The groundwater flow direction is approximately southwest at a shallow gradient of 0.0063 feet/
foot (ft/ft) Well surveying and correlation with existing shallow groundwater monitoring wells
provided data to establish groundwater flow direction. Groundwater in the vicinity of the TEM
property is represented by uneven groundwater elevation contours. This condition has potentially
resulted from local influences such as wet-season conditions and local infiltration from unpaved
areas adjacent to the investigation area and/or from recent sewer rehabilitation activities.

A well survey and sensitive receptor study of potential contaminant migration from TEM was
reported in July 2015 investigation report. This report noted an absence of downgradient
sensitive receptors that would be exposed to the offsite migration of hydrocarbon or VOC
constituents in groundwater. Downgradient land uses include freeway and railway corridors,
light and heavy commercial/industrial properties, and outdoor recreational uses. Figure 1
indicates the extent of former SF Bay margin areas that have been filled. The filled areas are
substantially underlain by historic municipal landfill debris which extends to the SF Bay
shoreline. There are no anticipated immediate or future impacts to the groundwater that might
affect current beneficial uses.

It is apparent that elevated concentrations of CVOCs, principally PCE, are present in
groundwater at the western margin of the property. It is Stellar Environmental’s opinion that the
extent of migration of PCE and related compounds has been reasonably concluded and that the
pathways of exposure have been addressed. The mass reductions of PCE and other VOC
constituents through the application of feasible treatment methods is anticipated to meet the
standard of care necessary to responsibly protect future beneficial uses of groundwater, the
environment, and human health.

LITHOLOGY AND HYDROGEOLOGY

Geologic and Geographic Setting

San Francisco Bay lies within a structural depression between the Diablo Range (East Bay Hills)
to the east and the Santa Cruz Mountains to the west. Within the structural depression, areas
between the bay and the mountain ranges are largely covered by Quaternary alluvium. This
alluvial covers the eastern flank of the San Francisco Bay structural trough to from about 3 to 9
miles from the bay to rock exposures in the Diablo Range. The alluvium and underlying
sedimentary units consist largely of late Pleistocene to Holocene unconsolidated marine and
continental deposits that contain the East Bay Plain Groundwater Basin. The underlying site
lithology consists of several feet of dark, organic, clay underlain primarily clay to silty clay, with
occasional interbedded silty to fine sandy clay and interbedded layers of gravelly clays, coarse
sand, and silty sand.

Groundwater flow direction and velocity are impacted by topography, geologic setting, and
stratigraphy. The general topography of the investigation area is gradually sloping to the west.
The underlying groundwater flows generally southwest–west toward San Francisco Bay as
indicated in previous and surrounding site studies.

Well surveying and correlation with existing shallow groundwater monitoring wells provided
data to establish groundwater flow direction. The groundwater flow direction is approximately
southwest at a shallow gradient of 0.0063 ft/ft. Groundwater in the vicinity of the TEM property
is represented by uneven groundwater elevation contours, which complicate the analysis of the
gradient. Figure 3 is shown with non-parallel contouring indicating local areas of groundwater
mounding, potentially influenced by wet-season conditions and local infiltration from unpaved
areas or from recent sewer rehabilitation activities.

Several observed conditions in the field suggest influences affecting the shallow groundwater
may include recent rain and wet conditions at the site and City of Berkeley rehabilitation of
sanitary drain lines and associated manways and lateral connections. These activities occurred in
the intersection of Park Way and Cedarwood Lane, at lateral connections to the TEM building, to



Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                          Page 4
the connection with the Gilman Street trunk pipeline. These activities included dewatering of
trenches and excavations filled with rainwater.

Other possible surface water influences to groundwater may be from the unpaved Park Way and
Cedarwood lane, the undeveloped portion of the west side of the TEM property and the railway
right-of-way to the west of the TEM property. Dry season monitoring and the absence of Wet
season conditions and construction activities may result in a more stable shallow groundwater
environment and clarify gradient conditions.

The deeper groundwater flow direction and gradient were not able to be measured due to the
linear orientation of the deeper wells and no comparable wells in the area, as is the case with the
shallow wells. Stellar Environmental expects the flow direction to be westward, towards San
Francisco Bay with little influence from seasonal rainfall or anthropogenic activities.

Historic representations of the pre-development margin the San Francisco Bay are indicated on
Figure 1. The former bay margin is located approximately 400 feet to the west of TEM. The fill
material from the eastern margin of the fill to the San Francisco Bay is generally recognized as
mixed municipal and construction waste.

Site Area Hydrogeology

This investigation focused on delineating the shallow and deeper water bearing units beneath the
site. Review of nearby monitoring wells and indications of water levels in selected borings
suggests that the shallow water-bearing zone is present in the depth interval of 5 to 18 feet below
ground surface (fbgs). Field logging of samples suggests clayey soils are present in the depth
interval of approximately 18 to 24 feet, though there is significant horizontal variability of soil
types.

The deeper groundwater-bearing zone appears to be present in the general depth interval of
approximately 28 to 36 feet. Clayey soils were previously investigated and appear in the depth
interval of approximately 32 to 40 fbgs.

The shallow-zone groundwater flow direction is approximately west to southwest at a hydraulic
gradient approximately 0.0063 ft/ft. These flow parameters are based on measurements obtained
from onsite and nearby groundwater monitoring wells. The deeper water-bearing unit is
suspected to be of similar gradient, though no wells are available to confirm this. Groundwater
elevations and flow directions for the shallow groundwater zone are represented on Figure 3The
calculation of the groundwater gradient was complicated by apparent anomalous concentrations
from monitoring well MW-16, which appeared significantly lower than characteristic elevation.
The complexity of the groundwater elevation contours suggested in Figure 3 was estimated by
the exclusion of MW-16. The influence of recent rainfall and significant construction work


Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                       Page 5
involving adjacent sanitary drain line repairs, including onsite lateral connections, have
potentially complicated groundwater flow. Future dry season groundwater monitoring may result
in stabilizing these impacts on the shallow groundwater flow conditions.

The shallow groundwater zone to approximately 18 fbg is well characterized by work performed
by Stellar Environmental and others. The shallow groundwater zone is consistently associated
with a sequence of silty sand, sand, and clayey sands at depths less than 20 fbgs. In most cases,
the first-encountered groundwater is observed at depths of less than 12 fbgs. The attached Photo
No. 12 is shows the soil type associated with a coarse sand layer of 2 to 3 inches in thickness
retrieved from the log interval of 28 to 30 fbgs at location MW-3D. This lens consists of a soil
interval with coarse sand and sand, underlain by a relatively homogenous silty sand and clayey
zone. Lithologic logs and well monitoring details by Stellar Environmental and others indicate
both the shallow and deep groundwater zones occur under confined or semiconfined conditions
as evidenced by a significant rise in the wells from the initial depth discovered. Stable
groundwater depths at the site are approximately 3 to 4 fbgs.


The offsite groundwater monitoring wells MW-14, MW-15, MW-16, and MW-17 were
completed to depths of 20 fbgs for the purpose of monitoring an offsite, upgradient, hexavalent
chromium release. These wells and the onsite monitoring wells MW-1S, MW-2S and MW-3S,
were used by Stellar Environmental to approximate groundwater flow direction at TEM.
Subsurface logging of soils suggests the first water bearing zone occurs in the approximate depth
interval of 8 to 16 fbg. Well development and sampling logs from April 2018 found the
stabilized groundwater depth to be approximately 3 fbg.

Firm to stiff, moderate to low plasticity clays are common in the lithologic descriptions noted
below the first groundwater zone and the deeper zone. These clayey soils are generally present in
the depth interval of 18 to 24 fbgs and suggest a potential barrier to the vertical migration of
contaminants. The deeper groundwater zone was identified during this investigation to be present
at depths between 24 and 36 fbgs. The deeper groundwater zone also appears to be under
confining conditions as groundwater recharge was often quite swift, resulting in depths of around
5 fbgs. This investigation consistently observed lateral continuity of this groundwater zone
between sampling locations.

Stellar Environmental was unable to obtain a groundwater sample from the approximate depth
interval of 32 to 40 fbgs at location GW-5B during the investigation of September 2016. This
depth was targeted based on previous work. This depth interval did not yield recoverable water
after being left open for approximately 4 hours. The presence of these clayey soils suggests a
thick, relatively competent impervious layer of soil is present below the deeper water bearing
zone.

Stellar Environmental Solutions                                                              Page 7
MIPS EXPLORATORY DRILLING

The MIP technology allows for dynamic screening the subsurface and providing real-time data
on conditions beneficial to the groundwater Treatment Application Plan (TAP). The use of MIP
technology for this project allowed rapid screening of the subsurface for VOC constituents. The
MIP technology provides insight into soil-type indicators, water-bearing zones, and the
subsurface distribution of VOCs in real time. This information allows refinement of the existing
CSM and provided data critical to the design and application of the selected remedial options.
While quantitative measurements of VOC concentrations are not possible with this technology,
these measurements identify subsurface conditions, presented in graphic form, to allow further
refinement of the conceptual site model and develop a targeted approach to the application of
treatment media.

The MIP technology provides real-time subsurface logging of subsurface conditions by
measuring temperature, conductivity, and volatile organic compounds. The instruments used to
detect VOCs are not quantitative in terms of concentrations in soil or groundwater but rather
relate relative concentrations passing the detector. The detectors used for this investigation
included:
 Electron Capture Detector (ECD). This detector is useful for the detection of halogens,
    phosphorous, and nitro groups. The detector uses a radioactive Beta emitter that ionizes
    carrier gas and measures the current between electrodes. The reduction of current between
    the electrodes is interpreted by the device and presented graphically.
 The halogen specific detector (XSD) operates by oxidizing halogen compounds and detecting
    halogens. This detector is useful in assessing the presence of CVOCs including PCE.
    However the XSD detector is not capable of differentiating halogenated compounds, it
    simply gives a reading of the total amount of halogen detected.
 Photo Ionization Detector (PID) continuously irradiates influent samples using a 10.2
    electron volt ultraviolet light. The current generated in this process is proportional to the
    compound concentration.
 Flame Ionization Device (FID) operates similarly to the PID however is uses a flame to
    ionize organic chemicals instead of an ultraviolet lamp. The breakdown of organic chemicals
    in this process produces ions that are measured and converted into an electronic signal.

The principal detectors used in this investigation to detect for the presence of PCE were the ECD
and XSD. The PID and FID identify organic compounds including petroleum products whereas
the XSD and ECD provide stronger indications of halogenated compounds, including PCE. The
presence of petroleum products at the site is well documented and these devices provide no




Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                     Page 8
differentiation between petroleum compounds and halogenated compounds such as PCE and
vinyl chloride (VC).

The MIPs exploration was conducted on March 29 and 30 2018 by Cascade Drilling of
Richmond California. Cascade Drilling, C-57 contractor’s license No. 938110, used a MIPs
direct-push track-mounted, Geoprobe™ model 7720 drilling rig, under the direct supervision of a
Stellar Environmental, California registered geologist.

Sample Location Rationale

The MIPs location rationale was presented in the September 2017 Workplan, being designed
primarily to rapidly measure soil chemistry and subsurface conditions to refine knowledge on the
fate and distribution of PCE and other VOC constituents in the subsurface. Five exploratory
MIPs were placed along the western-most margin of the property and at offsite locations in the
anticipated downgradient direction to the west, beyond the railroad right-of-way. These locations
were chosen to capture the northern and southern extent of impact to the subsurface as well as
define the distribution in the downgradient locations. Offsite locations were placed in the
anticipated downgradient direction of the principal areas of concern previously identified on the
TEM site.

MIPS data Findings

Five exploratory MIPs were advanced along the western downgradient margin of the TEM
property. Four MIPs were advanced to depths of approximately 40 feet. A fifth MIP was
advanced to approximately 50 feet in the northwestern area where elevated concentrations of
PCE were previously identified. The deeper bore, MIP M4, is designed to define the base of the
contamination. The onsite MIP locations were placed to evaluate the distribution of PCE and
related VOC constituents in soil and groundwater. MIP locations were selected on the basis of
data collected from previous grab-groundwater and soil samples. The MIP locations are
indicated on Figure 2. Two MIP locations, M6 and M7, were advanced off-site to depths of
40 fbg to evaluate potential impacts at locations presumed to be downgradient of the impacted
areas of the TEM property.

Stellar Environmental collected two grab-groundwater samples from MIP location M-6. This
location was selected based on the review of MIP logs M-6 and M-7. Location M-6 was chosen
on the basis of an apparently greater MIP probe response. Groundwater sampling and analytical
results for this work is described later in this report.

The subsurface interpretation of the distribution of PCE was further informed by the observation
that the subsurface stratigraphy does not show strong lateral continuity. Further, the presence of
VOC constituents is not defined by thick or massive zones, but rather by thin beds or lenses.


Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                      Page 9
Confined groundwater conditions have also been observed in both the shallow and deep zones,
which suggests mixing between lenses or bedding layers is likely. The probe detections of VOCs
in the subsurface do indicate stronger concentrations are present in the lower zone, which
appears to be consistent with the preliminary findings of the groundwater samples from
monitoring wells.

The MIP data suggest subsurface impacts occur in laterally discontinuous, thin, or undulate
lenses or laminations. Side-by-side comparisons of the MIP graphs for the ECD/XSD detectors
suggest subsurface impacts occur in thin, possibly inches or feet, lenses or layers. The detector
responses at MIP M4 show a significant VOC detector response on the XSD detector in the
depth interval of approximately 35 to 38 fbg.

This MIP investigation has further defined elevated VOC concentrations in the northern portion
of the study area. MIP detector indications from the northern-most portion of the site indicated
very little response, suggesting the extent of PCE impacts terminates at, or near, the northern
property boundary. The offsite MIP locations appear appropriately located to represent
downgradient conditions and no future monitoring of this area is recommended.

Shallow and deep grab-groundwater samples from offsite locations GW-14S and GW-14Deep
were collected adjacent to offsite MIP location M-6 as shown on Figure 2. These samples were
collected to characterize groundwater quality downgradient of the TEM property. MIP probe
logs for locations M-6 suggested a significant response over that for MIP M-7 on the PID/FID
and ECD/XSC detectors. MIP M-6 was also located in the anticipated downgradient direction
from TEM. These conditions formed the basis of for the selection of this location for the
collection of groundwater samples.

inside the outer probe casing to the depth of the bore and a groundwater sample was collected
using a disposable polyethylene bailer.

150 micrograms/liter (µg/L) while the shallow sample GW-14S was reported without PCE above

GROUNDWATER WELL DESIGN AND LOCATION RATIONALE

The MIPs site investigation data along the western border of the TEM facility was used to select
the screen intervals for the monitoring wells. As was reflected in the previous site investigation
work there appears to be two water bearing zones reflecting contamination that are divided by
intervals of little to no PID response in the MIPs. The MIPs PID response was also corroborated
by the MIP logs reflecting the higher permeable zone occurring predominantly between 5 and 20
fbgs and 30 and 40 fbgs. Those were therefore the selected screen interval of the shallow zone
and deeper zone wells. Six wells were installed in three nested pairs on the north, middle and
south side of the western border of the TEM facility as shown in Figure 2.

PCE and VC concentrations in the shallow zone ranged from 4.4 to 74 µg/L and not detected to
6.5 µg/L, respectively. PCE concentrations in the deeper zone ranged from 170 to 4,300 µg/L.
VC was not detected in the deeper-zone samples above the laboratory reported limits of
detection. The effects of the application of treatment media will be evaluated on the basis of the
results of future groundwater sampling events. The chain-of-custody form and soil sample
analytical report by Enthalpy are included in Appendix E. The results of this and previous
detections of PCE in soil samples are presented on Attachment F.

The monitoring well emplacement procedure involved the following steps:

The monitoring well emplacement procedure involved the following steps:
 Advancing 8.25-inch O.D. hollow stem augers to depths of approximately 21 and 41 feet
    below grade.

    milled-slot casing (well screen) in the deeper wells MW-1D, MW-2D, and MW-3D. 15-feet

    1 foot above the top of the well screens of the shallow wells.

 A 1-foot layer of 3/8-inch bentonite gravel was added on top of the filter-pack sand and
    hydrated.

 The wells were completed with steel, standpipes, approximately 32 inches above grade and

offsite monitoring wells for the purpose of estimating groundwater flow direction and gradient.

Laboratory Analytical Methods

The EPA analytical methods from Test Methods for Evaluating Solid Waste, Physical Chemical
Methods, SW-846 (EPA, 1986) were used to analyze samples during this project.

Groundwater monitoring samples were analyzed for site contaminants of concern as follows:
 CVOCs including TCE, PCE, and VC – by EPA Method 8260B for 8010 Analytes.

 Bioattenuation parameters: dissolved oxygen (DO), oxidation/reduction potential (ORP),
    total organic carbon (TOC), Iron (FE), and sulfate as well as standard parameters, pH,
    temperature, turbidity, and electrical conductivity.

The samples collected for this project were analyzed by Enthalpy Laboratory (Enthalpy) in
Berkeley, California. Enthalpy is a California and National ELAP-certified analytical laboratory
for all of the analytical methods required for the project. Groundwater samples were labeled,
dated, and stored in a cooler with ice maintained at a consistent temperature prior to delivery to
the laboratory. All samples were transported under chain of custody to Enthalpy and the analyses
were performed on a standard turnaround time.

CVOC Groundwater well Sample Results and Grab groundwater sample

The six groundwater monitoring well sample analytical results for CVOCs data are summarized
in Table 3. The certified laboratory reports and chain of custody are contained in Appendix E.

PCE was detected at a maximum 4,300 µg/L in the well MW-3D. This well is located in the
same area that two previous grab-groundwater sample submitted for analyses showed results of
28,000 µg/L PCE. The groundwater well data also confirms the previous findings that the site
COC, or risk driver, is the PCE compound. The VOCs TCE, cis-1,2-DCE and Vinyl Chloride
were also detected above their respective ESLs but at lower concentrations indicative of their
likely being daughter products of the PCE. Other detected VOCs were at trace concentrations or
at levels well below regulatory concern.

Stellar Environmental has used the reported values associated with the baseline groundwater well
sampling with the presumption that the consistently lower concentrations are more representative
of in-situ dissolved VOC conditions than were previous grab-groundwater samples.

Well sampling protocol decontamination before sampling was performed by Blaine Tech

a fenced secure location. 16 55-gallon drums of soil generated from drilling and well installation
activities were sampled by Blaine Tech on April 13, 2018. Sample analysis identified the soil as
non-hazardous and the soil was collected and transported for disposal by Baseline on May 23,

Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                     Page 18
4.0     CONTAMINANT DISTRIBUTION AND UPDATED
        CONCEPTUAL SITE MODEL

The results of this investigation confirm two distinct groundwater bearing zones and better
definition of the lithologic characteristics of these units. The shallow groundwater zone is
distinguished by a residual disseminated CVOC impacts, principally PCE with some indications
of TCE and trace indications of VC. The deeper groundwater zone is characterized by
occasionally strong indications of PCE. The PCE indications of the deeper zone now appear
most evident in areas recognized as associated with residual petroleum hydrocarbon impacts
from underground tanks and sumps.

This investigation focused on defining the characteristics of the deeper groundwater zone,
attempting to relate CVOC impacts to source areas, and further work to investigate upgradient
and offsite sources of the CVOC impacts noted in deeper groundwater zone. Significant potential
off-site sources included former UST cases, City of Berkeley complaint records alleging illegal
discharge of chemicals to the sanitary sewer system, and the presence of stormwater and sanitary
sewers flowing southward through and beneath the western margin of the TEM property.

Figure 5 shows a cross-section across the western portion of the property where the investigation
focused on the facility support area where historical sumps and USTs were located. Figure 5 also
depicts the underlying soil types are dominated by clay-rich material with low hydraulic
transmissivity. Discontinuous, 2- to 4-foot lenses or small channels of more permeable silts and
sands are significant in the depth interval from approximately 8 to 16 fbgs. PCE was reported in
previous investigations at a concentration of 28,000 µg/L in grab samples from both SB-2 and
GW-3B. These locations are located approximately 10 feet away from each other. Groundwater
samples collected during previous investigations suggest no significant offsite migration to
onsite areas as evidenced from samples collected at deep water zone sampling locations GW-9B
and GW-11B and from previous offsite sample locations SB3 and SB4.

The hydrologic character of deeper water-bearing zone appears to be relatively laterally
continuous and is now recognized (by the MIPs dataset) in a defined depth interval of
approximately 30 to 40 fbg at the TEM property. The deeper zone appears to be separated from
the shallow zone by an approximately 10-foot (20 to 30 fbgs) sequence of clayey soils. The base
of the deeper zone appears to consist of clayey soils as is evidenced by the lack of production of
water from GW-5 in the depth interval of 30 to 40 fbgs and as indicated at GW-3B in the depth
interval of 36 to 40 feet.


Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                     Page 19
The groundwater flow direction in the shallow groundwater zone is indicated to flow west to
southwest based measured new groundwater wells and selected WRE/Colortech wells in the
upper water bearing zone. While no WRE/Colortech deeper wells exist to calculate flow in the
deeper 30- to 40-foot wells and the alignment of the onsite wells do not allow for gradient
calculation, the flow direction and gradient in the deeper zone are expected to approximate that
of the shallow zone. Due to the relatively flat gradient, the groundwater migration velocity is
likely very low.

The data collected in this period both onsite and off-site do not assist in establishing any
evidence for any offsite source origins of the VOC contamination so the working CSM still
includes a “source” area near the wells MW-3S/D, although the mechanism of that source
introduction is still unknown with no known relationship to TEM facility operations. The
sanitary sewer line at depths of approximately 5.5 to 7.0 fbgs running north south through the
western area of the TEM facility as shown on the site plan figures was thought to be a potential
source given its documented lack of integrity but no evidence of that was found in terms of soil
and MIPs sampling data.

The data to date suggest the PCE impacts have originated in similar areas as did the petroleum
impacts, but with very different distribution results due to the different natures of the lighter TPH
versus heavier CVOCs. The footprint of the PCE appears to fit a scenario of narrow lateral
spreading with dissolved phase constituents evident in shallow groundwater, with concentration
in the deeper groundwater being higher, suggesting a relatively older plume to give sufficient
time for migration to the deeper zone.

SUMMARY OBSERVATIONS

It is the conclusion of this investigation that there appears to be PCE impacts in locations in
general association with historic underground tanks and sump. The presence of PCE and other
CVOCs has principally been recognized in sub-slab vapor, shallow and deep groundwater zones,
and with minor detections in soil samples. This investigation suggests a significant potential area
of elevated PCE concentrations is coincident with the historic location of underground petroleum
storage tanks and sumps located at the northern portion of the western margin of the TEM
property while previous investigations also suggest a possible secondary area of elevated
concentrations located in the southern portion of the western edge of the TEM property.

Groundwater CVOC Contamination Geometry and Migration Indications

The extent of the groundwater contaminant plume is determined by the mass of residual soil
contamination, hydrogeologic characteristics, and the ability of natural degradation mechanisms
to reduce contaminant mass. Groundwater contamination will continue to migrate downgradient
from the source area, primarily by advection with contaminant concentration reduction and also


Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                        Page 20
through natural biological attenuation. Shallow groundwater will likely continue to be degraded
by residual soil contamination by desorption from soil into groundwater.

The lateral extent of the shallow groundwater contamination is controlled by the permeability of
the soils; the hydraulic gradient, and anthropogenic influences. Dissolved contamination in
groundwater migrates in the direction of groundwater flow, likely to the west-southwest in the
shallow groundwater unit. Flow in the deeper unit would presumably flow similarly, though
would be less influenced by anthropogenic influences such as the Gilman Street storm drain
interceptor. Absent anthropogenic influences topographical slope to the west may more parallel
the flow of the deeper unit. In both units, groundwater flow would principally be westward.

In general, the natural attenuation of PCE does not appear to have progressed significantly as
there are few significant indications of degradation products including TCE and VC in
groundwater samples with significant PCE concentrations.

The downgradient extent of PCE and VOC impacts appears to be limited to the deeper water
zone, where sample GW-14Deep was reported with a concentration of 150 µg/L. PCE was not
detected in the shallow groundwater sample GW-14S. TCE was detected at a concentration of
1.4 µg/L at the shallow-zone sample location GW-14S. These downgradient sampling locations
appear representative of downgradient water-quality impacts of limited or no concern for
potential human or environmental receptors.

PCE Distribution Assessment

The result of this MIPs investigation, groundwater well installation and baseline sampling
corroborated earlier site investigation finding through grab groundwater samples that the PCE
detected in groundwater is at higher concentration at a depth of 30 to 40 fbgs than the upper
water barding zone at 5 to 20 fbgs. No new data on the source origins has merged however,
leaving the origins vague but clearly associated only with the western border of the TEM facility
where sumps and former UST were located, although no definitive indication of a source
associated with one or another of the USTs or sumps was found. No significant soil
contamination was found in previous investigations.

The current and previous vapor intrusion and indoor air assessments suggest no significant
potential risk of PCE vapor intrusion concern at the site.

LOW-THREAT CHLORINATED SOLVENT CASE CLOSURE POLICY
EVALUATION

An update of the Water Board LTCP evaluation will be completed following the in-situ injection
and post injection monitoring to determine its effectiveness in sufficiently reducing the residual
VOCs in groundwater to levels acceptable to achieve case closure.

Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                     Page 21
5.0     IN SITU BIOREMEDIATION DESIGN

The comparison of the previously collected grab-groundwater sample and the dissolved fraction
from the baseline well data suggest some of the PCE is sorbed onto colloidal particles as the well
data following development and purging showed lower concentrations of VOCs. Two previous
grab-groundwater samples the immediate area of MW-3D were both reported at 28,000 µg/L
PCE whereas well MW-3D showed 4,300 µg/L PCE in the baseline well sample. Both grab-
groundwater and well samples were collected from between 30 and 40 fbgs, the same screen
interval for well 3D. The difference is the Well MW-3D samples were collected after well
development and subsequent (3 days later) standard pre-sample well purging. The grab-
groundwater samples exhibited high turbidity and the PCE sorbed onto colloidal or soil particles
may explain the higher analytical result. The highest VOC concentration in the three shallow
zone (5 to 20 fbgs) wells was associated with MW-3S, at 160 µg/L total VOCs. A 10-20 foot
interval was selected for the shallow groundwater well intervals along with the bioremediation
injection interval because the 5-10 foot interval is too close the sewer line and base backfill
below it.

The remedial objective is to treat the higher concentration VOC dissolved plume area associated
with the 30 to 40-foot depth zone. While VOCs are also detected in the shallower 5 to 20-fbgs
zone it is at significantly lower concentration of < 200 µg/L total VOCs. The reductive
dechlorination in-situ remedy selected is designed to reduce the concentration of the PCE and
associated VOCs from sources unknown in the groundwater to below a concentration that will
meet the Water Board LTCP criteria if not its ESLs. The remedy seeks to achieve the remedial
action objective without the accumulation of dead-end intermediates (which is more prevalent
with the addition of simple carbon-only substrates such as emulsified oils). The proposed
remedial design accomplishes this through enhanced natural attenuation / biodegradation and in
situ chemical reduction (ISCR) uniquely induced via the use of the EDS-ER™ and Nutrimens™
compound.

The EDS-ER™ , EDS-QR™ and Nutrimens™ compound, along with KB-1 culture and Anoxic
Bioaugmentation Media will add a sufficient carbon source, augment microbes; total organic
carbon (TOC) concentrations greater than 20 mg/L are considered favorable for bioremediation
because they provide a carbon and energy source for microbes that participate in the
dechlorination reactions. The EDS-ER™, EDS-ER and Nutrimens™ compound will add >20
parts per million (ppm) TOC to the aquifer formation.



Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                     Page 22
The EDS-ER™ is an Electron Donor Solution Extended Release. EDS-ER is in the form of a
water-mixable oil; it contains no water. The bioremediation product is packaged in three
275-gallon totes, for a total of 2,100 net pounds. The EDS-QR™ (Electron Donor Solution -
Quick Release) is packaged in a 55 gallon drum 570 net pounds. The Nutrimens® is an all-
natural fermentation product. Nutrimens® liquid is produced during the anaerobic fermentation
of an unmodified strain of botanical classification Saccharomyces cerevisiae, including products
of fermentation, residual yeast cells and yeast fragments, and the media utilized during
fermentation. The Nutrimens™ is Packaged in a 55-gallon drum, totaling 520 net pounds.
Thirty-two Liters of KB-1 Culture and KI-Primer will be used as anoxic bioaugmentation media.
Reactions are extremely robust (effective under high or low DO/ORP conditions) but also
provide an effective bioremediation reaction over a period of 1.5 to 2 years or more. Appendix H
contains the Tersus product information and MSDS sheets.

The bioremediation product loading is based on the PCE and related VOC concentrations
detected in recently installed monitoring wells as well as previous grab-groundwater sample
indication of residual VOC locations. If the estimated amount of slurry per point is problematic,
the dimensions, mass requirements, mixing and other injection details can be readily modified in
the field based on site specific conditions (for example, the density of the slurry can be changed
to modify the total injection volume or the injection layout/number of injection points could be
altered depending on recommendations from the contractor).

EDS-ER™ EDS-QR™ and Nutrimens™ compound will be mixed with water at the surface and
delivered as a slurry across the saturated depth interval via injection utilizing a direct-push
Geoprobe™ rig. The Geoprobe™ rig and injection system equipment mobilized to the site for
the injection will consist of:
 Direct-push trac-mounted Geoprobe® rig.
 Drive rods (typically 1.5-inch outside diameter) and injection tooling with fluid delivery sub-
  assembly/
 Injection pump rated for 5 gallons per minute at 200 pound per square inch (psi) for sandy
  formations, and 800 psi for silt and clay formations.
 Injection hosing with pressure gauge and a pressure relief valve with a bypass.
 Power drill paint stirrer (3-inch-diameter or smaller propeller tip).
 Truck mounted mixing tank and hopper.
 Granular bentonite, quick-set grout concrete for closing and sealing injection holes.
 Water supply.


Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                     Page 23
 Electrical generator (if needed).

To accomplish the injection of the EDS-ER™ and Nutrimens™ compound product, the
Geoprobe® rig will advance 1.75-inch diameter, hollow, steel drive casing to the bottom of the
desired injection saturation interval. The casing will then be lifted approximately 1 foot to drop
the sacrificial drive point and expose the inner screened casing through which the product slurry
will be pumped. Water and product will be mixed to a slurry in a hopper at the surface. The
slurry will then be pumped from the hopper and down the casing, through the screen, and into
the formation at a pressure of approximately 200 psi.

The Tersus product loading assumptions use an average total VOC concentrations of 10,000
µg/L for the northern area around well MW-3D in the 30- to 40-foot interval and 500 µg/L total
VOC in the 10- to 20-foot injection zone around MW-3S. At the halfway point between the
nested S/D wells MW-2 and MW-3 the mass loading for the injection points in the deeper and
shallow zone will change from the 5,000 µg/L to 2,000 µg/L while the 500 µg/L total VOCs will
remain the same in the 10- to 20-foot injection zone as a conservative input parameter relative to
the baseline sampling results in the shallow wells.

The groundwater zone of apparent dissolved VOC impact is relative narrow along the west side
of the TEM facility so with a treatment radius 15 to 20 feet and the points staggered 5 feet
off-center. The approximate injection point locations are shown in Figure 6. The MW-3D zone
area using a maximum of 5,000 µg/L of VOCs (mostly PCE) produces a loading calculation is
26 pounds per vertical foot of the EDS-ER, EDS-QR™ and Nutrimens™ compound for the 10
borings. With 16 staggered injection points across two intervals totaling 40 (with different
loading) vertical feet.

6.0     CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

The work documented in this study was conducted in general accordance with standard EPA,
Water Board, and DTSC methods and protocols established for investigations of this type.

CONCLUSIONS
 It is Stellar Environmental’s opinion that the with the addtion of the MIPs data the extent of
    distribution and offsite attenuation of PCE and related VOC compounds has been sufficently
    determined to allow for in-situ bioremediation to proceed.
 The project area has been investigated and found to suggest a source area along the western
    portion of the TEM facility, particularly in the northwestern corner, that has no known source
    origins based on TEM operations.
 The CVOCs PCE, TCE, and VC have been detected in shallow soil (though only at trace
    concentrations), groundwater, and sub-slab gas at the TEM site. Offsite and upgradient PCE
    concentrations reported by others in the shallow groundwater suggested to be relatively
    consistent with other areas of industrialized west Berkeley. Shallow groundwater samples
    from offsite monitoring wells indicate a regional, non-specific, source for dispersed PCE,
    TCE, and associated VOCs with upgradient concentrations of PCE in shallow groundwater
    monitoring wells being reported in the range of 13 to 120 µg/L. This type of distribution of
    chlorinated solvents in the shallow groundwater is consistent with conditions observed in
    other commercial/industrial areas of west Berkeley.
 The northwestern portion of the site has PCE impacts in shallow groundwater and significant
    impacts to groundwater in a deeper zone observed below a depth of approximately 30 to
    40 fbgs. The shallow groundwater flow is approximately southwest, with some local
    variation, as reflected in the first groundwater well monitoring event, though continued
    monitoring should be performed seasonally to establish its consistency.
 The groundwater flow characteristics of the deeper groundwater zone are expected to be
    westerly, with a southern component and are not likely to be affected by anthropogenic
    influences.
 The sensitive receptor and well survey completed in June 2015 did not indicate the presence
    of a downgradient sensitive receptor that would be threatened by CVOCs detected in
    groundwater at TEM. A preferential pathway study has not been completed; however, the
    potential risk via migration of contaminants by way of anthropogenic pathways or conduits is


Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                     Page 26
    a possibility as there are storm and sanitary sewer pipelines in the subsurface of the project
    areas and adjacent to areas of significant impact.
 Offsite concentrations of PCE, TCE, and other CVOCs in both the shallow and deeper
    groundwater approximate concentrations recognized in shallow groundwater at TEM. As
    such, the VOC plume in the deeper zone from TEM facility appears to attenuate to a
    concentration not far removed from the west Berkeley ubiquitous VOC plume. The potential
    for migration from the deeper zone by preferential pathways or anthropogenic influences
    appears remote.
 Stellar Environmental has uploaded this report and associated data to the Water Board’s
    GeoTracker database and recommends following up with them following its receipt of this
    report to discuss the future needs to progress to regulatory case closure.

OPINION AND RECOMMENDATIONS
 The MIP and laboratory analysis of groundwater suggests the in-situ treatment pathway for
    groundwater is a viable means to progress to regulatory closure in agreement with the
    Chlorinated Low Threat Closure Policy;
 The offsite grab-groundwater samples show minimal impact indicating rapid attenuation in
    that direction and thus no groundwater wells are recommended to be installed there;
 Conditions are favorable for the application of in-situ treatment of groundwater in the deep
    and shallow zones.
 The bioremediation treatment media is recommended to be injected into 16 injection points
    at 10- to 20- and 30- to 40- fbgs intervals to reduce the identified VOC PCE contamination
    and daughter product concentrations using an average loading factor based on 500 µg/L PCE
    in the upper 10- to 20-fbgs zone and 10,000 µg/L PCE in the deeper 30- to 40-foot
    groundwater bearing zone;
 The success of the treatment alternative on the shallow and deeper groundwater-bearing
    zones will be evaluated through future onsite groundwater monitoring wells;
 The seven sub-slab vapor sampling ports that have been retained onsite have shown no vapor
    intrusion levels of concern and should be property closed with Water Board approval;
 Removal of accumulated groundwater waste that is currently stored onsite in 55-gallon
    drums is pending profile approval from the recycling facility;
 When sufficient reduction of CVOCs have been shown to have been achieved a new VOC
    low threat closure policy (LTCP) site regulatory closure assessment should be completed to
    achieve regulatory case closure; and




Stellar Environmental Solutions, Inc.                                                      Page 27
 All new data should be completed as a report for submission to the regulator and uploaded to
    the Water Board’s GeoTracker database.

This report has been prepared for the exclusive use of the subject property owners, TEM, its
authorized representatives, and the regulators. No reliance on this report shall be made by anyone
other than the client, client representatives, and regulatory agencies for whom it was prepared.

The information and investigative approach presented in this report are based on the review of
previous investigators’ findings at the site. This report has been prepared in accordance with
generally accepted methodologies and standards of practice of the area. The Stellar
Environmental personnel who prepared this report are qualified to perform such investigations
and have accurately reported the information available as of the date of this report, but cannot
attest to the validity of that information. No warranty, expressed or implied, is made as to the
findings, conclusions, and recommendations included in this report.

Site conditions may change with the passage of time, natural processes or human intervention,
which can invalidate the approach and methodologies presented in this report.

CONDITIONS OF APPROVAL:
     A. Applicant must possess a City of Berkeley Business License. Contact (510) 981-7200.
     B. Call the Toxics Management Division (TMD) at (510) 981-7460 and schedule an
        inspection of the grout sealing of boreholes, probes, or wells. Notify TMD a minimum of
        two (2) working days in advance of first scheduled day of drilling (review City holidays
        and reduced service days at http://ci.berkeley.ca.us/). Failure to notify staff of cancellation
        or delays may result in the applicant being billed for mobilization time.
     C. All borings must be properly destroyed (grouted/sealed) within 24 hours of drilling, unless
        special conditions are approved beforehand in writing as part of this permit, and must be
        continuously protected and stabilized.
     D. Proper storage, labeling & disposal of investigation-derived residual wastes are the
        responsibility of the consultant unless stated otherwise contractually. Wastes must be
        removed from the site within 2 weeks of conclusion of the drilling.
     E. Analytical results of all soil, vapor, and groundwater samples collected during the
        execution of drilling under this permit must be submitted to Toxics Management Division
        within 60 days of sample collection.
     F. A copy of the State DWR Form 188, boring logs, well construction details, and finalized
        as-built locations for all borings/wells (except geotechnical borings), must be submitted to
        TMD within 60 days of drilling/construction/destruction.
     G. Permit is valid for 120 days for the purpose specified herein. Construction aspects can be
        changed based on conditions encountered in the field. The permit is valid for only one
        TMD inspection.
     H. Wells installed under this permit may not be used for domestic, municipal, agricultural, or
        irrigation water supply.
     I. All work performed must conform to Business and Profession Codes and State Water
        Well Standards.
     J. The permit applicant and the property owner are required to ensure stormwater pollution
        prevention is implemented throughout the drilling process.
     K. Drilling company is required to contain all fluids and solids in compliance with stormwater
        pollution prevention rules. Any violation will lead to stop work, or cleanup order and
        potential enforcement.

 - CASCADE
Project Narrative
Cascade Technical Services (Cascade) is pleased to present this data report to Stellar Environmental
Solutions, Inc. for the membrane interface probe (MIP) services that were provided between the dates
of March 27th and March 28th, 2018 at your site located at 707 Gilman Street, Berkeley, California.

The results associated with the data and plots presented in this report were generated in accordance to
Cascade’s and Geoprobe’s Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for MIP services.

All field work and data management were completed by trained, scientific professionals and all quality
assurance/quality control (QA/QC) measurements associated with these data were found to be within
the tolerances set forth in the SOPs for these services. Response tests conducted previous to, and
subsequent to the MIP borings were found to be within the tolerances set forth for this MIP survey and
therefore the data are deemed acceptable for use. Exception/deviations regarding these response tests
and the related data are noted on the MIP Summary Table that is part of this report.

This report contains two sets of plots for each of the MIP locations; one set is scaled to show the lower
level responses based on the responses in each individual boring and the second set is scaled to show
the higher level detector responses.

I certify that the data package is in compliance with the terms and conditions of the contract, both
technically and for completeness, for other than the conditions detailed above. Release of the data
contained in this hard copy data package has been authorized by the laboratory manager or his
designee, as verified by the following signature.



Signature: ___________________________________

Daniel Caputo, Western Regional Manager of Site Characterization Services

MIP system.

            Ultra‐High Purity Hydrogen
MIP System Overview
The MIP is commonly used for quickly determining the locations of volatile organic compound (VOC)
source zones and plumes. The MIP is most valuable in terms of its ability to provide “spatial
correspondence”, meaning that where the MIP detector response show peaks, there is likely to be
elevated soil and groundwater concentrations. The MIP can also be used to provide extremely valuable
data to streamline subsequent investigative tasks and improve the overall efficiency and accuracy of the
site investigation. Vertical profiles, cross sectional views and 3D images of contaminant distribution can
all be produced from the electronic data generated by the MIP logs. The unique capability of providing
reliable, real‐time information allows for informed and timely decision making in the field. The MIP
works by heating the soils and groundwater adjacent to the probe to 120 degrees C. This volatilizes the
VOCs and allows the VOCs to transfer through a Teflon membrane via a combination of concentration
and pressure gradients. These VOCs are then swept into a nitrogen gas loop that carries these vapors to
a series of detectors housed at the surface. Continuous chemical profiles are generated from each hole.
Electrical conductivity of the soil is also measured and these logs can be compared to the chemical logs
to better understand the relationship between the lithology and the contaminant distribution. The MIP
technology is only appropriate for VOCs. The following section discusses the various detection systems
that are commonly used with the MIP system.
Detector Overview
             ECD – Electron Capture Detector uses a radioactive Beta emitter (electrons) to ionize some of
              the carrier gas and produce a current between a biased pair of electrodes. When organic

21
     CASCADE
          molecules contain electronegative functional groups, such as halogens, phosphorous, and
          nitro groups pass by the detector, they capture some of the electrons and reduce the current
          measured between the electrodes.
         XSD – The Halogen Specific Detector converts compounds containing halogens to their
          oxidation products and free halogen atoms by oxidative pyrolysis. These halogen atoms are
          adsorbed onto the activated platinum surface of the detector probe assembly resulting in an
          increase thermionic emission. This emission current provides a corresponding voltage that is
          measured via an electrometer circuit in the detector controller.
         PID – Photo Ionization Detector sample stream flows through the detector's reaction chamber
          where it is continuously irradiated with high energy ultraviolet light. When compounds are
          present that have a lower ionization potential than that of the irradiation energy (10.2
          electron volts with standard lamp) they are ionized. The ions formed are collected in an
          electrical field, producing an ion current that is proportional to compound concentration. The
          ion current is amplified and output by the gas chromatograph's electrometer.
         FID – Flame Ionization Detector consists of a hydrogen / air flame and a collector plate. The
          effluent from the GC (trunkline) passes through the flame, which breaks down organic
          molecules and produces ions. The ions are collected on a biased electrode and produce an
          electric signal.
MIP Data Collection
         Depth ‐ Data is collected every 0.05 feet, or twenty points per foot.
         Electrical Conductivity ‐ Electrical Conductivity data is measured/collected in milli‐siemens per
          Meter (ms/M). The conductivity of soils is different for each type of media. Finer grained
          sediments, such as silts or clays, will typically have a higher EC signal. While coarser grained
          sediments, sands and gravel, will typically have a lower EC signal.
         Rate of Penetration ‐ Rate of penetration (ROP) is measured/collected in feet per minute
          (ft/min). Speed is an indication of the advancement rate of the MIP probe. In order to allow
          for adequate heating of the MIP tooling, the MIP’s ROP should not exceed one foot per
          minute.
         Temperature ‐ Temperature data is measured/collected in Degrees Celsius. Temperature is an
          indication of the physical temperature of the MIP block. Minimum and Maximum temperature
          is collected at each vertical interval. Cascade's temperature protocol indicates that the MIP
          probe temperature shall maintain a minimum temperature of 90 Degrees Celsius.
         Pressure ‐ Pressure data is measured/collected in PSI. The pressure readings represent the
          pressure being delivered to the MIP’s nitrogen gas line. Deviations greater than of 1.5 PSI
          outside of the starting pressure indicate a system leak or obstruction is present.
         Detector (XSD, ECD, PID, FID) ‐ Detector responses are measured/collected in micro Volts (uV).
          Detector responses are an indication of relative contaminant responses. Minimum and
          Maximum detector responses are collected at each vertical interval.
Response Testing
Response testing (RT) is an integral part of ensuring the quality of data from the MIP system. Response
testing is conducted before and after each log. This ensures the validity of the data and the integrity of
the system. The RT provides a traceable indication that the MIP system detectors are adequately
responding and allows the carrier gas trip time to be calculated on the physical components of the
system.
Cascade uses acceptance criteria to evaluate the RTs. The acceptable criteria for an RT is defined for
specified concentrations of RT solution and a specified N2 trunkline flow rate. Documenting the RTs will

22
     CASCADE
provide a level of quality assurance for each MIP project and will also allow operators and data
reviewers to identify systems in need of maintenance.

The trip time is measured by recording the time between the moment when the VOA is placed over the
membrane and the response of the detectors, as viewed on the MIP data acquisition unit. The baseline
and peak response value are also recorded for comparison with other MIP response tests. The trip time
is entered manually into the data acquisition system account for the time it takes for compounds in the
subsurface to travel the length of the trunkline during the MIP boring.

                                               Data Qualifiers and Definitions
       Qualifiers
       A             See Report Comments.
       B             Analyte was present in an associated method blank.
       B1            Analyte was present in a sample and associated method blank greater than MDL but less than RDL.
       BQ1           No valid test replicates. Sample Toxicity is possible. Best result was reported.
       BQ2           No valid test replicates.
       BQ3           No valid test replicates. Final DO is less than 1.0 mg/L. Result may be greater.
       BQ4           Minor Dissolved Oxygen loss was observed in the blank water check, however, the LCS was within criteria, validating the batch.
       C             Possible laboratory contamination.
       D             RPD was not within control limits. The sample data was reported without further clarification.
       D1            Lesser amount of sample was used due to insufficient amount of sample supplied.
       D2            Reporting limit is elevated due to sample matrix. Target analyte was not detected above the elevated reporting limit.
       D3            Insufficient sample was supplied for TCLP. Client was notified. TCLP was performed per the Client’s instructions.
       DW            Sample result is calculated on a dry weigh basis.
       E             Concentration is estimated because it exceeds the quantification limits of the method.
       I             The sample was read outside of the method required incubation period.
       J             Reported value is estimated
       L             The laboratory control sample (LCS) or laboratory control sample duplicate (LCSD) was out of control limits. Associated sample
                     data was reported with qualifier.
       M             The matrix spike (MS) or matrix spike duplicate (MSD) was not within control limits due to matrix interference. The associated
                     LCS and/or LCSD was within control limits and the sample data was reported without further clarification.
       M1            The matrix spike (MS) or matrix spike duplicate (MSD) is not within control limits due to matrix interference.
       M2            The matrix spike (MS) or matrix spike duplicate (MSD) was not within control limits. The associated LCS and/or LCSD was not
                     within control limits. Sample result is estimated.
       N1            Sample chromatography does not match the specified TPH standard pattern.
       NC            The analyte concentration in the sample exceeded the spike level by a factor of four or greater, spike recovery and limits do not
                     apply.
       P             Sample was received without proper preservation according to EPA guidelines.
       P1            Temperature of sample storage refrigerator was out of acceptance limits.
       P2            The sample was preserved within 24 hours of collection in accordance with EPA 218.6.
       P3            Per Client request, sample was composited for volatile analysis. Sample compositing for volatile analysis is not recommended
                     due to potential loss of target analytes. Results may be biased low.
       Q1            Analyte Calibration Verification exceeds criteria. The result is estimated.
       Q2            Analyte calibration was not verified and the result was estimated.
       Q3            Analyte initial calibration was not available or exceeds criteria. The result was estimated.
       S             The surrogate recovery was out of control limits due to matrix interference. The associated method blank surrogate recovery
                     was within control limits and the sample data was reported without further clarification.
       S1            The associated surrogate recovery was out of control limits; result is estimated.
       S2            The surrogate was diluted out due to the presence of high concentrations of target and/or non-target compounds. Surrogate
                     recoveries in the associated batch QC met recovery criteria.
       S3            Internal Standard did not meet recovery limits. Analyte concentration is estimated.
       T             Sample was extracted/analyzed past the holding time.
       T1            Reanalysis was reported past hold time due to failing replicates in the original analysis (BOD only).
       T2            Sample was analyzed ASAP but received and analyzed past the 15 minute holding time.
       T3            Sample received and analyzed out of hold time per client’s request.
       T4            Sample was analyzed out of hold time per client’s request.
       T5            Reanalysis was reported past hold time. The original analysis was within hold time, but not reportable.
       T6            Hold time is indeterminable due to unspecified sampling time.
       T7            Sample was analyzed past hold time due to insufficient time remaining at time of receipt.
       Definitions
       DF            Dilution Factor
       MDL           Method Detection Limit. Result is reported ND when it is less than or equal to MDL.
       ND            Analyte was not detected or was less than the detection limit.
       NR            Not Reported. See Report Comments.
       RDL           Reporting Detection Limit
       TIC           Tentatively Identified Compounds
